articles.title: Bilhetes do CV apreendidos em presídio tinham 'conjunto de ordens' | G1
articles.standfirst: Os bilhetes tinham dados como uma tabela de preços das drogas dentro do presídio e orientações para os familiares dos faccionados. Dois presos foram autuados na delegacia.
articles.summary: Os bilhetes tinham dados como uma tabela de preços das drogas dentro do presídio e orientações para os familiares dos faccionados. Dois presos foram autuados na delegacia.
articles.body:
Os bilhetes do Comando Vermelho apreendidos na Unidade Prisional Elias Alves da Silva (UP 4) , no município de Itaitinga, na Região Metropolitana de Fortaleza (RMF), continham um "conjunto de ordens que organiza a disciplina interna, o mercado ilícito e a ofensiva contra o Estado" , de acordo com o juiz responsável por analisar a prisão de um dos dois detentos capturados com as mensagens.

As mensagens, apreendidas no dia 18 de novembro, traziam dados como uma tabela de preços das drogas dentro do presídio, orientações para os familiares dos faccionados e dicas a presos para fingir desmaios para distrair policiais.

O material estava em posse de um detento identificado como Rafael Rocha Lima, apontado como integrante do Comando Vermelho, mas as "diretrizes" teriam partido do "Conselho" da facção na UP4 - isto é, um grupo responsável pela tomada de decisões . Além dele, também foi preso João Bruno Nunes de Sousa. O g1 não localizou a defesa dos presos.

A Polícia Penal apontou que Rafael atuava no repasse desses comandos entre as diferentes alas dos presídios e que, em um dos bilhetes, constava como chave Pix para recebimento de valores o telefone da irmã de Rafael, que está em liberdade e é cadastrada como sua visitante no presídio.

Na audiência de custódia do preso, o juiz destacou que o suspeito "não portava um objeto proibido isolado, mas o conjunto de ordens que organiza a disciplina interna, o mercado ilícito e a ofensiva contra o Estado no estabelecimento prisional". Para a Justiça, inclusive, o fato dele usar a chave Pix da irmã evidencia a "existência de estrutura de apoio externa à unidade" .

Mensagens do CV apreendidas em presídios orientam simulação de desmaios e mobilização de familiares, no Ceará — Foto: Divulgação

Durante o banho do sol, Rafael Rocha foi visto tentando repassar pequenos pacotes envoltos em plástico. Ao perceber a fiscalização dos policiais penas, ele tentou ocultar os pacotes em uma estrutura de ventilação da unidade.

Parte do material caiu no piso, e toda a ação foi identificada pelo sistema de videomonitoramento da unidade prisional. Os policiais penais recolheram o material e encontraram uma série de textos com orientações de organização interna. Entre elas:

como deve ser a hierarquia da facção por ala;

centralização do controle das punições internas;

tabela de preços de drogas comercializadas na unidade.

Além disso, os textos também organizam uma ação coordenada contra a administração prisional. Entre as recomendações estavam:

a mobilização de familiares em liberdade, sob ameaça de sanção para aqueles que não participarem;

simulação de desmaios e aglomeração para forçar a saída de servidores das celas;

uso de advogados como canal de comunicação;

procurar veículos externos de comunicação para dar repercussão às denúncias e reivindicações dos detentos.

Parte das mensagens apreendidas com detentos membros do Comando Vermelho em unidade prisional em Itaitinga (CE) — Foto: Divulgação

Por meio de nota, a Secretaria de Administração Penitenciária disse que o material apreendido com Rafael vai ser usado para aprofundar as investigações, com objetivo de identificar os responsáveis pela elaboração do texto e "possíveis conexões externas".

Após apreender o material, os policiais penais levaram os detentos Rafael Rocha Lima e João Bruno Nunes de Sousa à Delegacia de Repressão às Ações Criminosas Organizadas (Draco), onde eles foram autuados. Rafael já responde pelos crimes de roubo majorado, por corrupção de menores e por homicídio qualificado.

"A ocorrência reforça a atuação da inteligência penitenciária e dos mecanismos de monitoramento e fiscalização da SAP no enfrentamento às organizações criminosas, na identificação de suas estruturas de articulação e na preservação da ordem e da segurança no sistema prisional cearense", complementou a Secretaria.

articles.title: Cox’s Bazar: Rohingya Life in Exile
articles.summary: Rohingya families face hunger, loss and an uncertain future during Ramadan.
articles.body:
Inside the world’s largest refugee camp, Rohingya families fight hunger and loss as aid dries up, clinging to faith, each other and the hope of returning home.

For more than a million Rohingya refugees, Cox’s Bazar was meant to be a place of safety. Instead, it has become a life on hold. Filmed entirely inside the camps in Bangladesh, this film follows six people: a widowed mother newly arrived from Myanmar, a father supporting his family through a small betel-leaf business, a student and advocate, an artist, a musician and a young man forced to conceal his identity for protection. Together, they face shrinking food aid, restricted opportunities, separation from loved ones and no clear route home. The Islamic holy month of Ramadan forms the backdrop, bringing moments of faith, family and communal ritual into sharper relief amid mounting hardship. Made with a Rohingya producer and director of photography living in the settlement, the film offers an intimate view from within: people working, studying, creating and caring for their families while fighting to preserve their dignity.

articles.title: Can we build a more ethical AI future?
articles.summary: Marc Lamont Hill speaks with tech entrepreneur Anil Dash about AI’s risks and the fight for ethical technology.
articles.body:
The artificial intelligence boom is transforming the global economy and concentrating enormous power in the hands of a few technology companies. But a series of developments is raising new questions about the industry’s stability and accountability from the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy to a wave of technology outages affecting the US government, major banks, companies and aviation systems alongside reports of hacked refrigerators across Europe. Concerns are mounting over the economic risks, mass layoffs, privacy and environmental impact of AI. And as AI company Anthropic began trading publicly, reaching a $2 trillion valuation, questions are mounting over whether the extraordinary levels of AI investment are sustainable. Is there a future where AI can be used for the collective good?

This week on UpFront , Marc Lamont Hill speaks with Anil Dash, former adviser to the White House Office of Digital Strategy in former United States President Barack Obama’s administration, about the risks of the AI boom, Silicon Valley’s growing political influence and the urgent need for greater accountability.

articles.title: Quem era o cabeleireiro encontrado morto dentro de casa no TO | G1
articles.standfirst: Paulo da Silva Dias, de 59 anos, era conhecido em Paraíso do Tocantins pelo carisma e pelo trabalho voluntário em ações sociais voltadas a pessoas em situação de vulnerabilidade.
articles.summary: Paulo da Silva Dias, de 59 anos, era conhecido em Paraíso do Tocantins pelo carisma e pelo trabalho voluntário em ações sociais voltadas a pessoas em situação de vulnerabilidade.
articles.body:
Cabeleireiro era conhecido como Paulinho — Foto: Reprodução/Prefeitura de Paraíso do Tocantins

O cabeleireiro Paulo da Silva Dias, de 59 anos, era conhecido em Paraíso do Tocantins , na região central do estado, pelo carisma e pela dedicação a causas sociais, conforme contou o amigo Joseilton Batista. Figura conhecida na cidade, Paulo foi encontrado morto dentro de casa, com marcas de faca, na última quinta-feira (19).

📱 Clique aqui para seguir o canal do g1 TO no WhatsApp

"Conheci o Paulinho cabeleireiro em 1992, logo após minha chegada ao Tocantins e fui morar em Paraíso. Me estabeleci abrindo uma livraria e um bar na mesma rua do salão de beleza dele. A partir daí ficamos amigos, ele era meu cliente e eu cliente dele", contou o jornalista Joseilton Batista, amigo de longa data do cabeleireiro.

Popularmente conhecido como "Paulinho Cabeleireiro", ele foi encontrado morto com marcas de faca dentro da própria casa. O corpo de Paulo da Silva foi sepultado na última sexta-feira (20).

O g1 questionou a Secretaria da Segurança Pública (SSP) sobre o andamento das investigações, mas não obteve retorno até a última atualização desta reportagem.

Segundo o jornalista, além de trabalhar diariamente no salão, Paulinho costumava prestar serviços voluntários em bairros periféricos de Paraíso do Tocantins, oferecendo cortes de cabelo gratuitos a pessoas em situação de vulnerabilidade social.

"Paulinho era amigo de todos e sempre ajudava em ações sociais nos bairros de Paraíso, cortando o cabelo da população mais carente. Era benquisto e eu nunca soube que tivesse algum inimigo ou desavença com alguém. Era sempre muito inteligente, bom nos negócios e muito cuidadoso nos relacionamentos", destacou o amigo.

A presença marcante do profissional também fez parte da infância e do cotidiano de moradores que viviam perto de seu salão e de sua casa. O morador Cleber, que conviveu com o cabeleireiro por cerca de 20 anos, destacou o vínculo afetivo que ele construiu com a vizinhança.

"Fui vizinho dele por uns 20 anos. Era uma figura carismática da nossa cidade. Eu me lembro dele desde quando era criança", contou.

Na ocasião, a Prefeitura de Paraíso do Tocantins lamentou a morte do cabeleireiro e manifestou solidariedade aos familiares e amigos.

articles.title: COP31: Brasil lamenta acordo final e cobra 'mais ambição' | G1
articles.standfirst: Conferência do Clima realizada na Turquia, que termina neste domingo (22), teve o principal acordo rejeitado pelos países. Presidente australiano admitiu que ficou "três noites sem dormir, negociando sem parar".
articles.summary: Com críticas da delegação brasileira e abandono da União Europeia, COP31 termina sem acordo após impasse sobre o financiamento e o fim dos combustíveis fósseis. Veja falas.
articles.body:
Embaixadora Liliam Chagas, da delegação do Brasil na COP31, discursa no último dia de negociações, em 22 de novembro de 2026. — Foto: Reprodução

Autoridades lamentaram neste domingo (22) o fracasso da COP31, Conferência do Clima da Nações Unidas (ONU) deste ano, que se encaminha para um final sem consenso entre os países participantes .

Na noite de sábado (21), já madrugada de domingo (22) em Antália, na Turquia, as presidências turca e australiana apresentaram uma versão do acordo final da conferência sem mencionar o fim dos combustíveis fósseis.

A reação dos países foi imediata, que consideraram o documento um retrocesso e prontamente rejeitaram o texto durante a plenária final da conferência.

A delegação brasileira, representada pela embaixadora Liliam Chagas, lamentou a falta de consenso entre os países e de ambição para combater as mudanças climáticas.

"Acreditamos que precisávamos de um espaço para abordar a sobrecarga climática, para aprimorar a ciência, triplicar o financiamento para adaptação, ter mais ambição no financiamento climático regional, para acolher uma agenda de ação reestruturada e para cuidar das pessoas vulneráveis", disse.

Na proposta de acordo, os presidentes da COP31 também deixaram de fora do texto o "mapa do caminho" , instrumento defendido pelo Brasil na COP30, realizada em Belém em 2025, e que previa a elaboração de um plano para orientar essa transição.

A sessão seguiu com duras críticas feitas pelos países. Em meio aos discursos, muitos também deixaram o local.

A União Europeia foi a primeira a formalmente negar a proposta, interrompendo a cerimônia e, logo em seguida, deixando o evento, argumentando que o resultado final "era uma vergonha".

A última vez que as negociações climáticas da ONU não conseguiram chegar a um acordo unânime foi em Copenhague, em 2009.

Presidentes da COP31 lamentam o resultado

A COP31 foi presidida por representantes da Turquia e da Austrália. Em uma edição marcada pela falta de consensos, ambos os países não conseguiram decidir nem quem tomaria a frente na edição deste ano, resolvendo-se pela dupla presidência.

Em meio à confusão na plenária, Chris Bowen, a liderança australiana, concedeu uma coletiva de imprensa do lado de fora da cerimônia, afirmando que o resultado era "decepcionante".

Aos jornalistas, Bowen explicou que a menção a combustíveis fósseis e financiamento climático foram os principais pontos que levaram ao impasse no texto final, admitindo ainda que tinha ficado "sem dormir nas últimas três noites, negociando sem parar, mas não funcionou".

"Uma questão óbvia é a transição para longe dos combustíveis fósseis, sobre a qual alguns países insistiram que deveria ser mencionada. Outras delegações insistiram que, se a expressão fosse inserida no texto final, vetariam a proposta", disse.

O presidente australiano da COP31 durante a plenária final do evento, em 22 de novembro de 2026. — Foto: Reuters

Durante a plenária, foi o presidente turco da conferência, Murat Kurum, que anunciou que não apresentaria nenhum novo texto e, posteriormente, deixou o palco em meio aos discursos dos representantes dos países.

Aos jornalistas, também em coletiva do lado de fora, Kurum admitiu o fracasso nas negociações.

"Alguns países, focados em uma única palavra ou frase, infelizmente dificultaram o processo ao levantar outras questões, questões não relacionadas às mudanças climáticas. Essa é a situação. Não há nada a fazer. Fizemos o nosso melhor. Agora que há tomadores de decisão, com 196 países envolvidos, eles tomarão a decisão. Portanto, respeitaremos a decisão deles", afirmou.

Presidente turco da COP31, Murat Kurum, fala a jornalistas em meio a plenária final da conferência, em 22 de novembro de 2026. — Foto: Reuters

Autoridades da ONU criticam falta de consenso

Simon Stiell, secretário-executivo de mudanças climáticas da ONU, também lamentou a falta de consenso entre os países na COP31.

Falando à imprensa no domingo (22), disse que, enquanto a conferência fica aquém do esperado, os efeitos das mudanças climáticas pioram.

"Compartilho da profunda decepção de muitos. A COP31 não conseguiu chegar a um acordo sobre questões relacionadas às decisões lideradas por ambas as presidências. O mundo não pode se dar ao luxo de que isso se repita."

Simon Stiell, secretário-executivo das Nações Unidas sobre Mudança do Clima (UNFCCC), fala no último dia de COP31, em 22 de novembro de 2026. — Foto: Reuters

Antônio Guterres, secretário-geral da ONU, disse estar "profundamente decepcionado" com a falta de consenso entre os países. "Compartilho da profunda frustração de todos aqueles que esperavam que os governos estivessem à altura das exigências da crise climática", disse.

Pelas redes sociais, o secretário-geral, que deve deixar a ONU no final deste ano, pediu que os países sigam enfrentando a crise climática, apesar do fracasso da conferência.

"Pode não haver consenso na sala de negociações, mas não há ambiguidade na ciência. A mensagem principal da COP31 é clara: o mundo precisa fazer muito mais para enfrentar a crise climática. E precisa fazer isso agora", afirmou.

articles.title: Cockroaches, dissent and a paradigm shift in India
articles.summary: The rise of the Cockroach Janta Party and what it reveals about the future of politics and journalism in India.
articles.body:
A youth-led movement born as online satire has unsettled Indian politics. Named after a dismissive remark by the chief justice, the Cockroach Janta Party has mobilised some of the country’s biggest protests in years. They have been driven by anger over exam leaks, unemployment and a lack of political accountability.

The demonstrators have been met by heavy police crackdowns and clashed with mainstream media outlets they accuse of serving the government.

As young Indians turn to social media and independent outlets to tell their stories, this film examines the growing divide between India’s youth and mainstream media and what it could mean for the future of politics and journalism.

articles.title: Vestibular Unesp 2027: Candidatos avaliam 1ª fase e citam química | G1
articles.standfirst: Estudantes ouvidos pelo g1 na Unip, em Ribeirão Preto, também citaram as questões em inglês. Gabarito oficial sai a partir das 19h deste domingo (22).
articles.summary: Vestibular Unesp 2027 reuniu 65 mil candidatos que apontaram exatas como desafio; confira detalhes sobre o gabarito oficial e as datas das próximas etapas.
articles.body:
Candidatos que fizeram a primeira fase do vestibular da Universidade Estadual Paulista (Unesp) neste domingo (22) na Unip, em Ribeirão Preto (SP), avaliaram a prova como tranquila ou dentro do esperado. As questões de química e a interpretação de textos longos foram os pontos mais citados como difíceis.

O g1 conversou com seis estudantes na saída do local de prova. O exame começou às 13h e teve 90 questões de múltipla escolha, com cinco horas de duração. Os candidatos podiam deixar o prédio a partir das 16h.

Ao todo, 65.706 candidatos disputam 5.850 vagas em 137 cursos de graduação. O gabarito oficial e o caderno de questões devem ser publicados a partir das 19h, no site da Fundação Vunesp, organizadora do vestibular.

O resultado da primeira fase está previsto para 7 de dezembro. A segunda fase será aplicada nos dias 13 e 14 de dezembro.

Candidatos aguardam a abertura dos portões para a 1ª fase do vestibular da Unesp em Ribeirão — Foto: Érico Andrade/g1

Gabriel Schiavon, de 27 anos, quer cursar educação física. Para ele, a prova da Unesp cobra mais conteúdo e desgasta menos que o Enem.

"Para quem estuda, tava fácil. É uma prova diferente do Enem, ela é menos cansativa. Ela cobra muito mais o conteúdo mesmo", disse.

Segundo Gabriel, quem revisou a matéria e manteve a calma conseguiu ir bem. Ele contou que acabou chutando a maioria das questões de exatas, porque não tinha revisado esse conteúdo.

Letícia Manchini, de 18 anos, também considerou o nível da prova fácil.

"Tinha muitas questões bem óbvias, mas eu gostei bastante de como eles intercalaram as questões com conhecimentos gerais, com conhecimentos um pouco mais técnicos. No geral, achei a prova bem tranquila", afirmou.

Aos 16 anos, Maria Eduarda Bram de Camargo ainda está no ensino médio e fez a prova como treineira. Ela quer cursar arquitetura e disse que reconheceu na prova conteúdos vistos na escola.

"Eu achei uma prova boa, ela não tava tão difícil. Muitas coisas que eu vi na minha escola caíram, algumas dicas que os professores deram", contou.

Candidatos correm para entrar na Unip antes do fechamento dos portões da 1ª fase da Unesp, em Ribeirão Preto (SP) — Foto: Érico Andrade/g1

Para João Fábio Meloni de Sousa, de 19 anos, as exatas foram a parte mais puxada. Ele quer cursar relações públicas e espera passar para a segunda fase.

"Eu achei que tava um nível um pouquinho elevado, mas nada muito além do esperado. Principalmente a parte de exatas tava um pouquinho mais pesada, mas deu certo", disse.

Letícia também apontou química como a área mais difícil. Gabriel afirmou que as questões da disciplina exigiam que o candidato estivesse "afiado".

Luisa Cruz Cirelli, de 17 anos, quer cursar ciências biológicas. Ela achou a prova fácil, mas cansativa por causa da quantidade de leitura.

"Tava muita interpretação de texto, acho que isso cansa mais. Textos muito longos cansam bastante", afirmou.

A estudante também teve dificuldade nas questões de inglês. "Eu sei inglês, mas não gosto muito. Tudo é inglês, o texto, as perguntas, tudo. Isso me complica um pouco."

America Aisling de Sousa, que quer cursar engenharia de alimentos, já prestou a Fuvest e edições anteriores do vestibular da Unesp. Para ela, a prova foi tranquila.

Candidata é abraçada antes de entrar para a 1ª fase do vestibular da Unesp em Ribeirão Preto (SP) — Foto: Érico Andrade/g1

"A impressão que eu tive é que os vestibulares estão ficando mais interpretativos", disse.

America também fez o Enem e avaliou que, em exatas, o exame nacional foi mais pesado que a prova da Unesp.

Gabarito: a partir das 19h deste domingo (22), no site da Vunesp

A Fundação informou que os horários e locais de realização das provas serão mantidos.A instituição também afirmou que adotará medidas administrativas e legais para apurar os fatos e responsabilizar as empresas envolvidas.

Em nota, a Caer informou que acompanha o caso e aguarda esclarecimentos oficiais da banca organizadora sobre as circunstâncias e os motivos da não aplicação das provas da tarde.

A companhia também informou que comunicará o ocorrido aos órgãos de fiscalização e controle e encaminhará a eles as justificativas apresentadas pela organizadora.

Comunicado sobre adiamento das provas do concurso da Caer foi colocado em locais de prova. — Foto: Arquivo pessoal

As provas para os cargos de nível superior, aplicadas na manhã deste domingo (22), foram mantidas. Segundo a Fundação, uma intercorrência registrada durante a aplicação foi pontual e não comprometeu a realização dos exames nem a regularidade do concurso.

articles.title: Homem é resgatado de escombros após ter casa destruída por tempo no RS | G1
articles.standfirst: Município foi atingido por uma supercélula com indícios microexplosão e ventos de 114 km/h na madrugada desta sexta-feira (20). Houve cinco mortes confirmadas.
articles.summary: Município foi atingido por uma supercélula com indícios microexplosão e ventos de 114 km/h na madrugada desta sexta-feira (20). Houve cinco mortes confirmadas.
articles.body:
Um homem e sua mãe foram resgatados por vizinhos debaixo de escombros da própria casa após o temporal que deixou um rastro de destruição em Tupanciretã , na Região Central do Rio Grande do Sul, atingir a casa deles. Eles ficaram feridos e foram transferidos para um hospital em Cruz Alta .

O município de Tupanciretã foi atingido por uma supercélula com indícios microexplosão e ventos de 114 km/h na madrugada desta sexta-feira (20). Houve cinco mortes confirmadas .

"Foi um momento muito feio, muito trágico. Foi uma questão de 20 minutos, devastou tudo. Foi caindo tudo e só o que eu pude fazer foi me abraçar na minha mãe e proteger ela e me proteger também", relata o aposentado Ezequiel Rodrigues Vargas.

Ele e a mãe foram resgatados dos escombros por vizinhos. Os dois e outras 20 pessoas foram transferidos para Cruz Alta. Ezequiel teve ferimentos e precisou ser atendido no hospital. Apesar do ocorrido, ele demonstra positividade com o futuro.

"Eu machuquei bastante a coluna, quebrei duas vértebras de costela, mas graças a Deus fui bem atendido no hospital de Cruz Alta. É tudo muito recente, mas graças a Deus a gente vai conseguir, vamos conseguir construir devagarinho, tijolinho por tijolinho no começo."

Relatos como o de Ezequiel dão a dimensão da força da tempestade que atingiu o Rio Grande do Sul na madrugada de sexta-feira (20). "Destruiu a cidade" , resumiu o prefeito Gustavo Herter Terra (PP). "Nível de destruição dramático" , atestou o governador Eduardo Leite (PSD). "Pensei que ia morrer" , relatou o cantor Alex Lopes.

Imagens aéreas mostra um rastro de destrição deixado pela supercélula. Uma empresa de sementes teve os silos destruídos e estima prejuízo milionário .

articles.title: Vagas de recenseador no Amapá: IBGE oferece salário de R$ 2,9 mil | G1

articles.summary: Vagas de recenseador no Amapá oferecem ganhos de até R$ 2,9 mil para candidatos com nível fundamental; inscrições no processo seletivo do IBGE seguem até 25 de novembro.
articles.body:
IBGE abre 58 vagas temporárias no Amapá — Foto: Divulgação/IBGE Goiás

Interessados em trabalhar no Instituto Brasileiro de Geografia e Estatística (IBGE) podem se inscrever para disputar uma das 58 vagas temporárias de recenseador disponíveis no Amapá. O prazo para inscrição segue aberto até o dia 25 de novembro.

As oportunidades são destinadas à coleta de informações em campo e fazem parte das ações do instituto para levantamento de dados estatísticos. Segundo o IBGE, a remuneração pode chegar a R$ 2,9 mil.

As 58 vagas estão distribuídas entre municípios do estado e destinam-se ao cargo de recenseador, responsável por visitar domicílios, aplicar questionários e coletar informações junto à população.

Os contratados receberão salário mensal de R$ 1.741, além de pagamento por produtividade. Com os benefícios, a remuneração pode ultrapassar os R$ 2,9 mil mensais.

Além do salário, os aprovados terão direito a auxílio-alimentação de R$ 1.192, auxílio pré-escolar, 13º salário proporcional, férias proporcionais com acréscimo de um terço e auxílio para deslocamentos.

Para participar, é necessário ter ensino fundamental completo. A seleção contará com prova objetiva marcada para 31 de janeiro de 2027.

O recenseador é o profissional responsável por realizar entrevistas e registrar informações estatísticas nos setores designados pelo IBGE. O trabalho é executado diretamente nos municípios atendidos pela seleção.

articles.title: Taxa de desemprego no Amapá cai e estado é destaque nacional | G1
articles.standfirst: Apesar de ainda ter uma das maiores taxas de desemprego do Brasil, o estado apresentou uma das reduções mais expressivas entre as unidades da federação.
articles.summary: A taxa de desemprego no Amapá recuou para 7,9% no terceiro trimestre de 2026, registrando a segunda maior queda do país segundo dados da Pnad Contínua do IBGE.
articles.body:
Carteira de trabalho digital — Foto: Marcelo Camargo / Agência Brasil

O Amapá apresentou uma das maiores reduções na taxa de desemprego do Brasil no terceiro trimestre de 2026, conforme dados divulgados na quarta-feira (18) pelo Instituto Brasileiro de Geografia e Estatística (IBGE), por meio da Pesquisa Nacional por Amostra de Domicílios (Pnad) Contínua.

Apesar de ainda figurar entre os estados com os maiores índices de desocupação do país, o estado amapaense registrou uma queda de 1,9 ponto percentual em relação ao trimestre anterior, desempenho que coloca o Amapá entre os destaques nacionais na geração de trabalho.

De acordo com o levantamento, a taxa de desemprego no estado ficou em 7,9%, atrás apenas de Pernambuco, que lidera o ranking nacional com 8,6%. Também aparecem entre os maiores índices Sergipe (7,4%) e Bahia (7,1%).

A redução observada no Amapá foi a segunda maior do país no período, ficando atrás apenas da Bahia, que registrou queda de 2 pontos percentuais. O resultado indica uma melhora no mercado de trabalho amapaense, embora os desafios ainda permaneçam.

articles.title: Californian Call of Duty cake call that started new line of work
articles.summary: Kimberley Neequaye, from Derbyshire, says she ignored the call when Activision first approached her.
articles.body:
When a cake maker received a call from California asking if she could make a cake to mark the 20th anniversary of the Call of Duty video game, she thought it was a joke.

But it proved to be a genuine call from the tech firm Activision, and since then her cakes have become more and more popular in the gaming world.

The American company went on to order another similar cake to mark the release of a new version of the Call of Duty game , and this week an IT firm ordered a cake to celebrate the launch of Grand Theft Auto 6 .

Kimberley Neequaye, 44, from Hadfield in Derbyshire, said she had ignored the call when Activision first approached her.

"My phone just rang and it was an unknown number and it came up (as from) California and I thought 'there's no way I'm answering that, that's going to be a scam'," she said.

"Then an email came through and I was just (thinking), this is bizarre.

"When I found out it was the actual creators of Call of Duty, it was just mind-blowing."

She does not know why the company chose to get in touch with her, but thinks they simply googled "cake makers near Manchester".

The initial order was placed in 2024, and although Activision's headquarters are in Santa Monica in California, the cake was for staff at its office in Manchester - to mark the 20th anniversary of Call of Duty.

Last month a representative from the company emailed asking her to make a cake for about 20 staff in the Manchester office to mark the release of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4.

The cake she made was on an 18-inch board and included a helmet, a belt of bullets, a hand grenade and games controller.

"I wish I'd actually recorded the reaction I got when we walked into the office, because the staff were just amazed," she added.

"It was massive. I had to keep stopping and resting. The cake was so heavy."

It went down well because she got a follow-up email saying "it looked incredible and the team was really happy".

This week she also delivered a decorated cake to Inology, an IT firm based in Tameside.

Kimberley said staff had seen photos of her other work and wanted a cake to mark the release of the latest Grand Theft Auto game.

Kimberley has not always made cakes for a living - there have been two shifts in her career.

"I went to uni, got my degree (because I) wanted to be a teacher," she said.

"And then I just decided on a whim - because that's what I'm like - that I didn't want to be a teacher anymore."

So she bought the bakery and cafe where she had worked as a teenager in Glossop.

Then she changed her career again after her high street business closed during the Covid pandemic.

She decided to focus on making cakes from home and now bakes them from her converted garage in the village of Hadfield.

The fact she is building a name for herself as a cake maker, who specialises in video games, has taken her by surprise.

"I don't even have a game console," she added.

"My son's only just started playing on games - we're more of an outdoor family and we go fishing quite a bit."

articles.title: Newsom and Biden overruled thousands of jurors with the stroke of a pen
articles.summary: Gavin Newsom spared 548 California death row inmates on Nov. 5. He waited till he had one foot out the door.
articles.body: Not all murders are eligible for the death penalty. In fact, murder alone is almost never sufficient for society’s ultimate punishment. It must be murder plus what we call an aggravating circumstance, such as the murder of more than one person, the murder of a child or a murder in the commission of another crime, such as burglary, rape or robbery. In the universe of capital-eligible cases, very few death sentences are sought and even fewer are given. For those given, the process is rightfully arduous. The prosecution must convince the jury of both the underlying crimes and that death is the proper sentence. Those are separate trials. In other words, 12 people must agree, beyond a reasonable doubt, twice before anyone can be sentenced to death. And the return of the death verdict is only the beginning of the appellate process. There are direct appeals, collateral appeals and challenges to everything the police, prosecutors, defense attorneys and judges do and say. And even though I handled seven death penalty cases to verdict, I full well understand those who are opposed to capital punishment and have spent no time trying to change their minds. To serve on a death penalty jury, each potential juror is questioned individually about his or her beliefs, background and understanding of the law. You get some interesting answers in these individual voir dire sessions. I have heard potential jurors say, "I don’t think I could give death to someone who killed in self-defense." That’s encouraging to hear, since killing in self-defense is not even a crime. I would hope no one could sentence a person to death for something that was not even criminal. Other potential jurors have said, "I could give it, but only if I witnessed the killing." You realize that if you did actually witness the killing, you would be a witness and not a juror, right? Same answer for those who said, "I could only give the death penalty to someone who killed a family member or a friend." Understandable, but you would be ineligible to serve on a jury if either of those were true. In sum, capital cases are usually reserved for the worst offenders who commit murder plus an aggravating circumstance. For most of the cases in which I was involved, no one "gave" the defendant the death penalty. They earned it. It was a lifetime achievement award for raping, robbing and victimizing other people over the course of decades. GAVIN NEWSOM WIPES OUT CALIFORNIA'S DEATH ROW IN HISTORIC MASS COMMUTATION California Gov. Gavin Newsom is ineligible to serve on a death penalty jury. He claims he is morally opposed to the sentence, but more on his "morality" in a bit. He is likewise ineligible for extralegal reasons to be the chief executive of this country. In an act of reckless temerity, he cleaned out California’s death row. Five hundred forty-eight convicted murderers sentenced to death by California juries were let off death row by the governor on Nov. 5. As reported by Fox News Digital, the governor "will spare the lives of 548 inmates currently on the state’s death row, effectively clearing capital punishment in the state years after issuing an executive moratorium on executions." Did Gov. Newsom do this when his name was on the ballot? Of course not; that would require conviction and principle. He did it on the way out the door when there would be no political fallout (or so he thinks). CALIFORNIA DA SAYS GAVIN NEWSOM'S 'CRUEL' DEATH ROW CLEMENCY STABS CRIME VICTIMS 'IN THE HEART' Did he consult the families of all the victims? Doubtful. Did he carve out exceptions for the most depraved inmates? Of course not. Did he carve out exceptions for those who had incurred additional infractions while incarcerated? By no means. Even former President Joe Biden (presumably it was him) left the person who murdered nine Black Christians in a South Carolina church on federal death row. HAWLEY ERUPTS AT BIDEN PARDON ATTORNEY OVER DYLANN ROOF CLEMENCY PUSH Biden commuted 37 of the 40 federal inmates on death row. What he did is no less egregious than what Newsom did; it was just political pandering because of how public the killings of the three remaining inmates were. He left the man who killed nine Black Christians, he left the Boston Marathon bomber, and he left the man who killed 11 people at a Pittsburgh synagogue. For all the talk about the rule of law, both men ignored it by singlehandedly overturning the will of 585 juries. Even allowing for the occasional bench trial in capital cases that represents overturning the will of thousands of women and men who had carefully weighed and balanced the aggravating and mitigating circumstances and found that the crimes committed so shocked the conscience as to warrant society’s ultimate punishment. NEWSOM’S DEATH-ROW COMMUTATIONS SPARK DA REVOLT AS PROSECUTORS WARN OF LEGAL FIGHT For all the talk about anti-democratic acts, what could be more anti-democratic than summarily overruling the will of people who sacrificed their time, their employment, and their innocence to listen to and view horrific fact patterns? NEWSOM REVEALS WHEN HE'LL DECIDE ON 2028 WHITE HOUSE BID AMID GROWING SPECULATION Were the men Newsom spared factually or legally innocent? Of course not. If they were, they would not have been on death row to begin with. If he believes any of those men were factually or legally innocent, he should have commuted their sentences long ago. CALIFORNIA PROSECUTORS SLAM NEWSOM'S DEATH ROW COMMUTATIONS, ACCUSE GOVERNOR OF PUTTING 'POLITICS OVER PEOPLE' Both Biden and Newsom waited until the last minute to undo what over 7,000 people had voted unanimously to do. People can have whatever views on capital punishment they want to have. That is none of my concern. I have family and friends who feel passionately on both sides of the issue. articles.title: North Carolina farmer Noah Ranells chose 'Only the land lives forever' as his yearbook quote, and now he has permanently protected 63 acres of his farm in a county that lost 18% of its farmland in a decade
articles.summary: Do you still believe, or even remember, what you wrote in your yearbook? What you write in a yearbook can follow you much further than you might imagine.
articles.body: Do you still believe, or even remember, what you wrote in your yearbook?What you write in a yearbook can follow you much further than you might imagine. For Dr. Noah Ranells, a farmer from North Carolina, the words “Only the land lives forever,” which he listed in his high school yearbook, have grown into more than just a personal philosophy. They seem almost prophetic, as he has now taken steps to protect the very farmland he has spent years working on, ensuring it remains preserved for generations to come.Piedmont Land Conservancy, in a report dated November 17, 2026, informs readers that Ranells has permanently protected 63 acres of Fickle Creek Farm in Alamance County, North Carolina, through an agricultural conservation easement established on November 12, 2026. This agreement was made with Piedmont Land Conservancy, alongside the Alamance County Soil and Water Conservation District and North Carolina's Agricultural Development and Farmland Preservation Trust Fund.A farm that has been part of a lifelong ambitionThe land at Fickle Creek Farm is home to more than grazing cattle and open pastures. Its fields support a variety of wildlife, with goldfinches and field sparrows moving between trees and fence lines, while insects fill the surrounding landscape. Grass-fed Senepol, Angus and Red Poll cattle graze across the property in the early morning, finding shade in the nearby woodland before noon.For Ranells, farming was not an ambition that developed much later in life. He grew up in rural Pennsylvania as one of seven children in a family involved in 4-H, a youth development programme through which he spent time showing dairy cattle, goats and sheep at county fairs. According to Piedmont Land Conservancy, he also recalls receiving a blue ribbon for a white patty pan summer squash, although working with livestock was what eventually drew him more strongly towards agriculture.By the age of 12, he already knew that he wanted to be involved in farming for the rest of his life. His journey towards this ambition was further shaped by teaching animal science through the Peace Corps and completing a PhD in Crop and Soil Sciences before eventually establishing a farm with a partner.Importance of protecting farmland in Alamance CountyAccording to USDA Census of Agriculture figures cited by Piedmont Land Conservancy, the county lost 18% of its farmland between 2012 and 2022, representing nearly 15,000 acres. The loss of agricultural land is not simply about a reduction in the number of working farms, but also about what happens to the land that once supported them.Once agricultural spaces are converted for development, returning them to their former use can become difficult, if not impossible. Ranells has expressed concern about this very issue, describing agricultural land as a non-renewable strategic asset and pointing out that once it is paved over, it does not come back.An agricultural conservation easement is a long-term legal commitment that places restrictions on how a property can be used, particularly to prevent its development. This agreement ensures that the land remains protected for agricultural purposes and can continue to be available to farmers for generations to come, rather than being converted for other uses.Keeping the connection between food and the land aliveFickle Creek Farm does not operate in isolation from the communities around it, with its produce and other goods reaching customers across several parts of North Carolina.Ranells and his team reportedly deliver meat, eggs and vegetables to homes between Burlington and Raleigh. They also sell their produce at farmers' markets in Chapel Hill, Durham and Morrisville, while customers can visit the farm to collect their orders directly.This relationship between the people who grow food and those who consume it reflects an idea that Ranells admires in the work of American writer and environmentalist Wendell Berry. Berry, who died this year at the age of 92, wrote extensively about farming communities, local economies and the relationship we share with the natural world. One of his best-known observations was that eating is an agricultural act, an idea that connects everyday meals to the land, farmers and agricultural practices behind them.For Fickle Creek Farm, maintaining that connection means continuing to produce food on land that is cared for, while allowing customers to remain connected to the people responsible for growing it. The protection of this property is therefore important for safeguarding a part of the local food system that has developed around the farm.A promise for the foreseeable futureRanells' decision to protect the 63 acres is also shaped by how he imagines the property being used long after his own time as its farmer. He hopes that someone working the land a hundred years from now will have discovered the right balance for grazing, maintaining pastures that remain healthy and productive throughout the year.The identity of the future farmer is not something that needs to be determine today but what matters to is that the opportunity to work the land will continue to exist.A land embodies the world we inhabit, having sustained generations of humans, livestock and countless other species. When Ranells wrote “Only the land lives forever” in his high school yearbook, perhaps the most remarkable truth was already encoded in those words: that the land can continue to sustain generations to come, provided we choose to care for it.You use AI every day. articles.title: Children in besieged Gaza struggle to find life-saving insulin for diabetes
articles.summary: Insulin and blood glucose testing supplies become increasingly difficult to obtain in war-torn Gaza.
articles.body:
Gaza City, Gaza Strip – When Amir, a nine-year-old with diabetes, began repeatedly vomiting and complaining of severe abdominal pain, his mother, Nahawand, called an ambulance. He was rushed to a hospital in Gaza City and admitted to intensive care, where doctors found a dangerous build-up of acid in his blood due to insulin poisoning.

Nahawand said last week’s hospital admission was the latest and most frightening consequence of a struggle to find enough insulin to keep Amir alive and his blood sugar under control.

Amir was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes when he was just a year old. His mother has to monitor his blood sugar throughout the day and adjust his insulin according to his readings and meals.

Keeping Amir’s condition under control with diabetes medication has become increasingly difficult due to the high cost of insulin caused by Israel’s crippling siege on Gaza and because her husband is out of work.

After months of being unable to find insulin in Gaza City, 39-year-old Nahawand finally managed to obtain supplies brought from Khan Younis, in southern Gaza, only to discover the medicine had expired.

“I cannot afford to buy it. I am unable to buy insulin for my son at all,” she told Al Jazeera.

Before the war, Nahawand said a single insulin pen cost between 25 and 30 shekels (($7.62 to $9.17), or was free through clinics and aid organisations. Now a pen costs between 50 and 80 shekels ($15.29 to $24.46).

His mother checks his blood sugar roughly every two hours, as well as before meals, to determine whether he needs insulin. Depending on Amir’s readings and what he eats, he may require two or three injections a day.

But the test strips needed for these checks have also become increasingly unaffordable, between 150 and 200 shekels ($45.87 to $61.17) for a box of 50. Before the war, Nahawand could buy two boxes for about 150 shekels ($45).

“Our children are already living with an illness,” she said. They should not have to suffer like this on top of it. Insulin is not too much to ask for.”

The International Diabetes Federation (IDF) said in August that it was “deeply concerned by the severe restrictions on access to insulin and essential diabetes care in Palestine”. It noted that access to diabetes care is particularly severely constrained in Gaza.

Awni Shweikh, executive director of the Haifa Association for Children with Diabetes, said her organisation speaks on behalf of about 800 children with diabetes in Gaza and appealed for urgent supplies of insulin pens and blood glucose testing strips.

Established in 2012 as the first association in Palestine dedicated to children with type 1 diabetes, Haifa used to provide a free box of testing strips every month to as many as 700 kids.

They also supplied insulin pens for children, offered educational sessions for families, provided psychological support and insulin to families not covered by UNRWA services. But since the start of the genocidal war in Gaza in October 2023, children lost their blood glucose monitoring devices and there was a severe shortage of insulin pens, threatening their lives.

“Insulin is not a luxury. It is a life-saving treatment,” Shweikh told Al Jazeera.

Some families have been forced to use expired insulin, resulting in kids being admitted to hospital with dangerously high blood sugar levels and complications involving acidity in the blood.

The loss of testing strips created a second, closely connected problem: even when parents managed to find insulin, they could not always measure their children’s blood sugar or determine the correct dose.

Alaa Ghaban, who lives with her family in a school for displaced Palestinians in Jabalia in northern Gaza, said insulin shortages have affected her daughter’s health and appetite.

Fifteen-year-old Janna was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes when she was just eight and needs two types of insulin, one taken during the day and another at night. Her thirty-six-year-old mother said she cannot stop either medication, but with supplies difficult to find and prices rising, securing both is a constant struggle.

One type of insulin that previously cost around 30 shekels ($9.17) now costs about 80 shekels ($24.46). But with no regular income, even reaching organisations that previously helped is becoming unaffordable.

Janna feared that eating without having enough insulin to control her blood sugar could be dangerous, so over the past four months, she has lost seven kilos.

“She has become afraid to eat because she is afraid she will wake up and not find insulin,” Alaa said.

Janna was recently admitted to hospital for eight days, malnourished and dehydrated, with tests showing high acidity levels in her blood and an enlarged liver.

Alaa once had to return to her family home under heavy Israeli bombardment to retrieve life-saving insulin for her daughter. Keeping medication cool is another daily challenge due to electricity shortages.

“My daughter sometimes wishes she were dead because she cannot bear watching us struggle and seeing me exhausted,” she said.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia intercepts drone, missile as Houthis report attack on Sanaa
articles.summary: Houthi media say several people were injured in an attack on an oil company as Saudi air defences down a drone.
articles.body:
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis in Yemen says it has intercepted a drone and a missile launched by the Houthis, while the media affiliated with the Yemeni group reported that at least six people were wounded in an air attack on an oil company’s fuel station in Sanaa.

The Yemen News Agency quoted the spokesperson for the Ministry of Health and Environment, Anis al-Asbahi, as saying on Sunday that Saudi aircraft targeted a fuel station operated by the state-run oil company on 60th Street, “injuring six employees and causing material damage”.

There was no immediate comment on the claim from the Saudi-led coalition fighting against the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God).

Separately, the Saudi-led coalition spokesman, Turki al-Maliki, said the country’s air defences destroyed a drone launched by the Houthis towards the Saudi capital, Riyadh.

Al-Maliki did not provide further details or report any casualties or damage in his post on X.

His statement came hours after he announced that a ballistic missile was intercepted and destroyed as it targeted the country’s western region, on the coast of the Red Sea.

Saudi Arabia’s western region has key energy infrastructure, including the Yanbu oil terminal, a facility for crude exports, and the Jazan refinery in the far southwest of the country, which borders Yemen.

The Houthis have attacked oil installations in Saudi Arabia in recent weeks, along with airports and military sites.

Meanwhile, clashes continue between the internationally recognised Yemeni government forces and the Houthis on several fronts, amid warnings of worsening displacement and food shortages.

Since seizing Sanaa in September 2014, the Houthis have controlled much of northern and western Yemen, and the internationally recognised government has controlled much of the south. While a United Nations-brokered ceasefire largely halted the fighting in 2022, the conflict flared again this summer when the Houthis announced a blockade on Saudi ports.

The group then carried out a lightning offensive in September, seizing much of Yemen’s Red Sea coastline near the Bab al-Mandeb strait. Government forces launched a counteroffensive last month to recapture territory from the Houthis, but forces allied to the government earlier this month said they would withdraw from areas around the strait and focus on defending Aden.

Analysts say the conflict is no longer driven solely by the dynamics in Yemen , and it is intertwined with the wider regional confrontation and the US-Israel war on Iran.

Houthi attacks have killed 26 people in Saudi Arabia since September, including 23 in strikes on airports, according to the kingdom’s authorities.

On Thursday, a tower housing the headquarters of Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund in Riyadh’s financial district sustained damage on several floors in a Houthi attack, authorities said.

A skyscraper belonging to state oil giant Aramco was also damaged in a strike at the beginning of the month.

articles.title: Prince William may let daughter Princess Charlotte give up royal titles; 11-year-old dreams of pursuing a career on stage, already earning admiration for acting and singing talents
articles.summary: Princess Charlotte could have a future away from royal duties, with reports suggesting that Prince William plans to give his younger children the freedom
articles.body: Princess Charlotte could have a future away from royal duties, with reports suggesting that Prince William plans to give his younger children the freedom to choose their own paths when they grow up. The Princess of Wales and William's daughter is reportedly keen on pursuing a career in the performing arts, with her talents as an actress and singer already earning admiration from those around her.According to a report in the Daily Mail, citing claims from royal author Tom Sykes's forthcoming book, Dukes of Hazard, William intends to give Princess Charlotte and her younger brother, Prince Louis, the option of relinquishing their royal titles and HRH styles once they reach adulthood. This would allow them to build independent careers and lives outside the responsibilities associated with being members of the Royal Family.Princess Charlotte is reportedly passionate about acting and singingAt 11, Charlotte is said to have already demonstrated considerable talent on stage through school productions. A source quoted by the Daily Mail described her as a natural performer, saying, "She belongs on the stage. She's a wonderful actress and singer and that's what she wants to be when she grows up."Her reported interest in acting has also drawn comparisons with her great-grandmother, Queen Elizabeth II, who enjoyed performing in her younger years. The late monarch participated in wartime pantomimes at Windsor Castle. Her grandfather, King Charles III, also had an interest in theatre and performed comedy sketches with the Dryden Society drama group while studying at Trinity College, Cambridge.Her choice of school may reflect her love for performing artsCharlotte's reported ambitions are said to have influenced her preference for secondary education. Sources cited in the report claim that she is interested in attending a prestigious boarding school known for its performing arts programme.The school is reportedly equipped with its own theatre, stages several major productions every year and offers drama scholarships to talented students. It also hosts professional touring productions, giving pupils an opportunity to experience theatre beyond the classroom.Charlotte currently attends Lambrook School, where her younger brother Louis is also a pupil. Her next educational move is therefore expected to be an important decision for the young royal.Kate Middleton has encouraged Charlotte's interest in music and danceCharlotte's love for performing arts is not entirely new. The Princess of Wales has previously spoken about her daughter's musical interests. During a visit to the Vsi Razom Community Hub in October 2023, Kate revealed that she had heard Charlotte singing the song Shine Jesus Shine that morning, adding that it had made her very happy.Kate had also spoken about Charlotte's enthusiasm for dance when she was just two years old. During a 2017 visit to Kensington Palace, she told English National Ballet director Tamara Rojo that her daughter was taking dance lessons and "absolutely loves it".The mother-daughter duo have also shared an interest in theatre. In 2022, Kate took Charlotte to watch Mary Poppins in London's West End, where the young princess reportedly met the show's star, Zizi Strallen, backstage.More recently, Charlotte and Kate were spotted travelling on London's Elizabeth Line and getting off at Tottenham Court Road, close to the capital's theatre district. The outing is believed to have been for a theatre visit.Why Charlotte and Louis could have the freedom to choose their own futuresWilliam's reported approach to his younger children is believed to reflect the parenting style of his aunt, Princess Anne. Anne chose not to give her children, Peter Phillips and Zara Tindall, royal titles, allowing them to pursue careers and interests outside the formal structure of the monarchy. Zara became an accomplished equestrian, while Peter has built a career in business and sports management.Similarly, Prince Edward and Sophie, Duchess of Edinburgh's children, Lady Louise Windsor and James, Earl of Wessex, are entitled to use HRH styles but do not generally use them.According to the report, Charlotte and Louis also do not routinely use their royal titles at school and are not formally addressed as "Your Royal Highness" by staff at home.Prince George, however, is in a different position. As William's eldest child and the future heir to the throne, his royal responsibilities are expected to be considerably different. Royal author Tom Sykes reportedly describes George's future role as something that is "set in concrete".For Charlotte, however, the possibility of choosing a different path could open up opportunities to explore her interests without the expectations of a working royal. articles.title: An Alabama woman supported her husband while he trained as a surgeon, but their divorce excluded his medical-business interests from marital assets; an appeals court reversed that division and ordered a new review
articles.summary: An Alabama appeals court has overturned part of a divorce settlement after finding that a lower court wrongly excluded a surgeon's medical-business
articles.body: An Alabama appeals court has overturned part of a divorce settlement after finding that a lower court wrongly excluded a surgeon's medical-business investments from the couple's marital assets. The woman had worked and helped meet household expenses while her husband completed medical training. The case has now been sent back for a fresh assessment of the couple's property.Sarah Gordon and Charles Gordon married in 2011, the year Charles completed medical school. He subsequently underwent an internship, a five-year orthopaedic surgery residency and a spine-surgery fellowship. During this period, Sarah worked as a nanny and took up other jobs to help pay household expenses.Charles completed his fellowship in 2018, after which the couple moved to Baldwin County. He joined Baldwin Bone and Joint, an orthopaedic practice, and became a partner in 2020 or 2021 after borrowing money from First Horizon Bank. Sarah, meanwhile, became a full-time homemaker and had no separate income.In its November 20, decision, the Alabama Court of Civil Appeals ruled that the husband's business interests should have been considered marital property. It reversed the property division and directed the lower court to determine their value and reconsider the distribution. However, it did not specify what share Sarah should receive.Financial disputes during divorceSarah filed for divorce in February 2024. The trial court subsequently ordered the couple to maintain their existing financial arrangements and prohibited them from disposing of assets acquired during the marriage without permission.Sarah later accused Charles of restricting her access to bank accounts and credit cards. She also alleged that he had withdrawn around $183,000 from their joint checking account.Under a temporary agreement adopted by the court in October 2024, Charles was required to place the withdrawn money in an interest-bearing account, resume depositing his salary into the joint account and transfer another $20,000. He was also directed to restore Sarah's access to their financial accounts.Sarah subsequently alleged that Charles had issued three cheques totalling $19,400 after depositing the additional money. She also complained that he had again restricted her access to the joint account.Charles admitted during the trial that he had stopped depositing his salary into the account around May 2024 and again around February 2025. He also acknowledged removing Sarah as an authorised credit-card user, saying her spending exceeded what he could afford.Court rejects request to postpone trialIn October 2025, Sarah sought $30,000 towards expert assistance and legal expenses, saying she needed professionals to examine her husband's assets.The final hearing was scheduled for December 8, 2025. Three days before the trial, she sought a postponement, saying she could not afford a forensic accountant and had recently discovered a bank account and credit card for which she had not received records.The trial judge rejected the request, noting that the divorce case had been pending since February 2024.The appeals court upheld that decision. It said Sarah had raised the need for expert assistance in October but waited until shortly before the hearing to seek a postponement. Her lawyer had also failed to explain what an accountant might discover or how the findings would affect the case.Medical businesses should be included The main issue in the appeal was Charles's ownership interests in Baldwin Bone and Joint, a surgery centre and other medical consulting businesses.During the trial, Sarah submitted an assessment estimating that Charles's 15.38% interest in Baldwin Bone and Joint Medical Center, LLC, was worth $219,491. The calculation was based on a September 2025 balance sheet.The lower court admitted the document but treated the business as Charles's separate estate. It also declined to accept a tax document relating to the surgery centre as a valuation. Charles had invested $150,000 in that centre but maintained that its shares were "worth nothing" because the business was operating at a loss.The appeals court found that the business interests had been acquired during the marriage. Charles completed his medical training seven years after the wedding and purchased his medical-practice partnership interest in 2020 or 2021. There was no evidence that he had acquired these interests before marriage or received them through gifts or inheritance.Under the law, property accumulated during marriage can form part of the marital estate. The appeals court said the lower court had no sufficient evidence to classify the businesses as Charles's separate property.Charles argued that the lower court had already accounted for the investments through a $70,000 property settlement awarded to Sarah. However, that payment covered several matters, including retirement-account adjustments, moving expenses and his violations of earlier court orders.The lower court had neither valued the businesses nor specified how much of the settlement was intended to compensate Sarah for them. The appeals court therefore found that the payment did not correct the error in excluding the businesses from the marital estate.Home, vehicle and alimony issuesThe appeals court also addressed the couple's marital home. The lower court had recorded its equity as $100,000, describing the figure as an agreement between the parties. Sarah disputed this and argued that the equity was $150,000, based on a $1.5 million appraisal and a $1.35 million mortgage.The appeals court found no clear agreement on the amount and directed the lower court to determine the equity from the evidence.It also ordered the lower court to consider the Mercedes G-Wagon, which had been excluded because it belonged to an LLC, alongside the valuation of the business interests.The court left the decision not to award Sarah a vehicle unchanged because she had testified that she did not hold a valid driving licence at the time of the trial.It also allowed the lower court to reconsider alimony after completing the revised property division, as the two issues are connected.The appeals court upheld the refusal to postpone the trial and the decision not to hold Charles in contempt or impose additional sanctions.It ultimately reversed the division of marital property and sent the case back to the Baldwin Circuit Court. The lower court must now value the medical-business interests, include them in the marital estate and reconsider an equitable division of the couple's assets.You use AI every day. articles.title: Hull's modernist landmarks highlighted by interactive tour
articles.summary: Hull's post-war buildings are brought to life in a new interactive guide.
articles.body:
Hull's modernist, post-war landmarks are being brought to life in a new interactive tour.

The city now appears on The Modernist app, an architectural guide produced by the Modernist Society, which celebrates 20th Century design.

Along the route, which is nearly 2.5 miles long, walkers encounter some of Hull's best-known mid-century landmarks, including the Cecil Cinema, the former Hammonds Department Store and the Three Ships mural.

Charlotte Tomlinson, who created and photographed the tour, said the city had "picked itself up and [been] rebuilt with real ambition" following World War Two.

Hull suffered extensive bomb damage during the war, which led to decades of rebuilding.

"I wanted these tours to help people stop, look more closely and appreciate the craft and optimism in buildings that are too often taken for granted, and to show visitors a side of Hull they won't find in the usual guidebooks," Tomlinson said.

Fans of 20th Century design will be able to tour the city's bold civic buildings, modernist designs and striking public artworks via a map of photographs alongside historical background notes.

According to the Local Democracy Reporting Service , the tour takes roughly 90 minutes on foot, although the route can also be browsed remotely.

The Modernist app was launched with tours of Manchester in 2024 and has grown to include Glasgow, Sheffield, Huddersfield, Bristol and Liverpool. Hull is the eighth city on the app.

articles.title: Luana Lopes Lara, 30, spent 14 to 16 hours a day building Kalshi into a $40 billion prediction market giant; now she faces a legal battle over alleged violations of US state gambling laws
articles.summary: At 30, Luana Lopes Lara has achieved what many entrepreneurs spend a lifetime working towards.
articles.body: At 30, Luana Lopes Lara has achieved what many entrepreneurs spend a lifetime working towards. The co-founder of prediction market platform Kalshi has become the world's youngest self-made female billionaire, and she says her success is the result of relentless ambition, hard work and an unusual appetite for challenges.Lara launched Kalshi in 2021 with her co-founder Tarek Mansour. The US-based platform allows users to trade contracts based on the outcomes of real-world events, including politics, sports, the economy and other developments. What started as an ambitious business idea has grown into a major player in the prediction market industry.According to reports, Kalshi's valuation rose from $11 billion in December 2025 to $40 billion by October 2026. Speaking to The Sunday Times, Lara opened up about her approach to work, the sacrifices behind her success and the mindset that helped her build the company."I really take a lot of pride in doing the absolute best that I can. I want to see how far I can go, how much I can do, how big I can be," she said.Luana Lopes Lara's demanding daily routine and approach to successLara's work ethic is central to how she approaches entrepreneurship. She reportedly wakes up at 5.30 am and spends between 14 and 16 hours at the office, working six days a week. She describes herself as someone who handles several responsibilities simultaneously and remains optimistic even when things become difficult."At work I am doing a hundred things at the same time at every point in time," she told the publication. Describing her attitude towards challenges, she added, "I'm the very optimistic, positive one. I'm very much, like, 'The odds are in our favour, let's go, we're ripe.' I have to be fine no matter what's happening."For Lara, difficult circumstances are not necessarily a reason to step back. In fact, she says she finds a certain satisfaction in taking on challenges that others might consider too difficult."I'm a little weird because when there are more sacrifices, somehow in my brain that is a good thing," she said, recalling the years she and Mansour spent trying to get regulatory approval for Kalshi."When it was four years of hell to get regulated, there was a part of both Tarek and I that liked how hard it was - because it was like we were doing an important thing."From mathematics Olympiads to intense ballet trainingLara's competitive streak developed long before she entered the world of business. As a child, she participated in mathematics and astronomy Olympiads and was accustomed to setting exceptionally high standards for herself.She recalled how even a near-perfect score was not enough to satisfy her."For me, I need to get 100 [in tests]. If I got 99.99 it is terrible, it is the end of the world," she said.She also described herself as stubborn, someone who enjoys arguing and debating. However, one of the biggest influences on her determination was her years of rigorous ballet training.Lara recalled the intense and sometimes disturbing environment in which she trained, describing how instructors would resort to extreme measures to push performers."[The instructors] would break glass and put it in other girls' shoes," she said. She also recalled instances in which dancers had parts of their costumes taken away, making it difficult for them to return to the stage.Reflecting on how those experiences shaped her, Lara said, "I've always had a somewhat easier time doing things that look very unlikely and are very painful in nature."How Lara and Tarek Mansour fought to get Kalshi approved in the USBuilding Kalshi was not straightforward. When Lara and Mansour first developed their business idea, the company faced regulatory restrictions that prevented it from operating in the way they envisioned in the United States.In November 2020, Kalshi received approval from the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), becoming the first federally regulated prediction market of its kind in the country. However, the approval came with restrictions on certain categories, including terrorism, assassination, war, gambling and illegal activities.Politics and sports were initially excluded from its offerings. When Kalshi launched in July 2021, it had around 30 markets, largely focused on subjects such as the economy, weather and Covid.Lara, however, believed that politics and sports would eventually become important parts of the business. Betting on political outcomes had faced longstanding legal restrictions in the US, but she was determined to challenge them.According to The Sunday Times, she found a lawyer willing to take up the fight when most others were reluctant. The company reportedly held more than 30 meetings with the CFTC, repeatedly facing rejection before eventually securing a breakthrough.In 2024, Kalshi won its legal battle over political event contracts, opening the door for users to trade on election outcomes. The platform subsequently became a significant part of political coverage in the US.Kalshi expands into sports and faces regulatory scrutinyFollowing the legal victory, Kalshi expanded its presence in sports markets, including contracts linked to the Super Bowl. The company also increased its visibility through sports sponsorships and advertising, including its association with the US Open.Its rapid growth has also brought political attention. Donald Trump Jr reportedly joined Kalshi as an adviser and received shares in the company. However, the company later announced that his advisory role had ended following a significant investment by his firm in a competitor.A Kalshi spokesperson said the two sides had mutually agreed to end the arrangement, adding that the company appreciated his contribution in helping introduce the platform to more customers.Kalshi has also attracted criticism over the nature of its business. Several US states have challenged the platform, arguing that its event-based contracts resemble gambling and should be subject to the same regulations as betting companies. More than 20 states are reportedly involved in litigation concerning prediction markets.The company has rejected the comparison. Lara has maintained that Kalshi is not a gambling platform, despite criticism over the risks users face. According to the company's own data cited in the report, around 74 per cent of its users lose money.The platform has also faced questions about insider trading and market integrity. One prominent case involved former US congressman George Santos, who was banned from the platform after allegedly making more than $17,000 betting on whether he would attend the State of the Union address. Santos denied wrongdoing.More recently, Kalshi has faced further regulatory scrutiny over markets linked to political figures and their statements, while lawmakers have called for stronger oversight of prediction markets.Luana Lopes Lara says building Kalshi is her dream come trueDespite the controversies, regulatory battles and intense demands of running a rapidly expanding company, Lara remains committed to the business she helped create.Her journey from a competitive student and ballet trainee to the co-founder of a multibillion-dollar company reflects an approach built around ambition, persistence and an appetite for difficult challenges."This is my dream come true and I am not going to complain about it," she said. "I am going to do everything I can for it to work."For Lara, the long working hours and sacrifices are part of the journey rather than the price of success. And with Kalshi's growing reach, she appears determined to see just how far she and her company can go.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Workers began carving “1776” into Mount Rushmore in 1930; a design change halted the planned history inscription, and the date was later removed
articles.summary: Discover the fascinating history behind Mount Rushmore's original design, including the unfinished '1776' inscription and the vision of sculptor Gutzon Borglum. Learn why this significant feature was never completed.
articles.body: Mount Rushmore is famous for its four presidential faces, but the original design included another major feature: a large inscription about American history. Workers began carving the date “1776” into the mountain in 1930 as the first part of this plan. But the modification of the sculpture and worries about its legibility led to reconsideration of the plan by Gutzon Borglum. It was never placed on the mountain; rather, at a later date, the sculptor was intended to place the inscription in a room behind the sculptures. It was thought of by Gutzon Borglum, the sculptor responsible for directing the Mount Rushmore monument project in South Dakota. He intended that the monument should depict the history of the country and the reasons for choosing the four presidents. This inscription was named the Entablature.The original plan included a giant historical inscriptionBorglum intended to carve the Entablature into an area beside the presidential figures. The space was situated in the Louisiana Purchase territory and the letters were supposed to stand about 3 feet tall. According to the National Park Service’s account of the Entablature, the inscription was meant to commemorate the first 150 years of the United States. It described the nine important events between 1776 and 1906. Borglum thought that president Calvin Coolidge would aid him in writing the inscription, but they differed on how to phrase it and Coolidge passed away in 1933, before they could reach a compromise. Another contest of essays led to yet another version of the text; nevertheless, Borglum did not approve of it. Work had already started. In 1930, “1776” was inscribed on the eastern side of Mount Rushmore. The purpose of this inscription was to represent the start of history. This inscription was the only one from the Entablature to be carved on the face of the mountain.Moving Jefferson changed the designThe positioning of the president became altered while the monument was being constructed. In 1934, Borglum realised the need to shift the face of Thomas Jefferson from the right-hand side of George Washington to his left-hand side. This alteration affected the Entablature’s designated space. The designated space meant for the inscription had to be used for the sculpture of Abraham Lincoln. Borglum also felt that the huge inscription would not be readable by people viewing the monument from below. Due to these issues, the original plan could not work and hence Borglum thought it necessary to shift the historical record concept to a planned hall behind the presidents’ sculptures called the Hall of Records. The inscription “1776” was removed later.The Hall of Records also remains unfinishedThis hall was supposed to have some documents related to US history in order to show the story of the country. Work started in 1938. Tunnels were approximately 21 m into the granite wall behind the sculpture figures. But the work stopped in 1939, after Congress ordered that money should be spent to finish the heads of presidents. Gutzon Borglum died on March 6, 1941, without completing this structure. According to the National Park Service, the completion of this memorial was done under the guidance of Lincoln Borglum on October 31, 1941.Eventually, the miniature version of the archival idea was implemented. On August 9, 1998, a vault housing 16 porcelain and enamel panels was put in the entrance of the Hall of Records. These panels describe the creation of the memorial, its sculptor and the reason for the four figures of presidents. The Entablature was never completed and the Hall of Records remained unfinished. Four faces of presidents became the hallmark of Mount Rushmore, but the plan of Gutzon Borglum was not implemented in full. The National Park Service’s history of the Hall of Records and its historical study of the project document how the original inscription plan evolved.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient.
