articles.title: Remembering Fiona: Timeline of how the hippo beat the odds, became a star and inspired millions
articles.summary: From a 29-pound preemie to a global star that inspired millions around the world, the Cincinnati Nile hippo Fiona boosted zoo attendance before her sudden death. Here's a timeline of her life.
articles.body: Millions of Americans are mourning the loss of Fiona. The 9-year-old Nile hippo who captured the hearts of people all over the country after surviving an early birth in January 2017 and becoming the world's first premature hippo to be raised by humans died at the Cincinnati Zoo and Botanical Garden on Thursday, Nov. 19, after ingesting a visitor's knitted hat that was accidentally deflected into her enclosure. Born six weeks early at just 29 pounds, Fiona rapidly drew enthusiastic online followers. She also helped push annual attendance at the zoo as fans traveled from far and wide to catch a glimpse of the spunky creature. Her death occurred roughly a decade after another high-profile demise at the same zoo, when Harambe, a 17-year-old western lowland gorilla, was fatally shot by zoo staff in May 2016 after a young boy climbed into his enclosure. BELOVED HIPPO FIONA DIES AT CINCINNATI ZOO AFTER SWALLOWING VISITOR'S HAT The Cincinnati Zoo on Friday released new autopsy findings after Fiona's death. A postmortem examination determined that a foreign object, confirmed to be a hat that zoo officials said accidentally wound up in her enclosure, was lodged deep inside the hippo's massive digestive tract, according to the zoo's director of animal health, Dr. Mike Wenninger. The hat was lodged halfway through her small intestine, roughly 25 feet past her stomach and still 50 feet from exiting her body. Zoo visitors, local and federal leaders, and fans all around the world are still trying to absorb news of the animal's passing. "I was really mad," a young woman in downtown Cincinnati told Fox News Digital on Friday. "I know it was a fluke accident… but it just seemed like it could have been prevented in some way. And she was just so iconic. This is just devastating to the community." Fiona came into the world under extraordinary circumstances. The woman added, "I was really upset. I went home from work after that." Fiona has had books written about her, murals painted of her and even clothing with cute depictions of her created in her honor. The city of Cincinnati has considered her its unofficial mascot. Here's a timeline of Fiona's life Jan 2017: Fiona is born Fiona came into the world on Jan. 24, 2017, under extraordinary circumstances. The hippo was born six weeks before she was due. She "was too small to stand and nurse from her mom, Bibi," according to the Cincinnati Zoo. She weighed a mere 29 pounds at birth — 25 pounds lighter than the lowest recorded birth weight for Nile hippos, according to the zoo. "The zoo's care team had to step in and figure out how to feed her, what to feed her, how to keep her warm, and how to manage critical care 24/7 while juggling other daily responsibilities," the zoo's website states. "It took a village, but #TeamFiona did it!" Fiona's father, Henry, was 35 years old when she was born (he died in Oct. 2017). Bibi was 17. Fiona was the first Nile hippo to be born at the Cincinnati Zoo in over 50 years. Jan 2018: Fiona weighs in at 650 pounds Fiona experienced a big year of growth in 2018. LOCH NESS MONSTER SIGHTINGS JUMP IN 2026 AS SCIENTIST DRILLS INTO LEGENDARY MYSTERY By her first birthday, Jan. 24, 2018, she tipped the scales at 650 pounds. She also attracted a lot of attention during this period. "By sharing her ups and downs with the world (every day for almost two years), she became a beloved symbol of hope and a source of inspiration for millions of people," the zoo's website states. By her third birthday in January 2019, she weighed half a ton — with zoo officials describing her as a "thousand-pound toddler." August 2022: She welcomes a half-brother Fiona's half-brother, Fritz, was born to Bibi on Aug. 3, 2022, fathered by a male named Tucker. BABY ELEPHANT MAKES HISTORIC ARRIVAL AT SMITHSONIAN'S NATIONAL ZOO AS FIRST BIRTH IN NEARLY 25 YEARS The zoo documented when Fiona and baby Fritz first met three weeks later. "Five-year-old Fiona was curious but took her cues from her mom, Bibi, and backed off when Fritz got almost close enough for a nose boop," the zoo said. "This first intro went very well. Bibi was appropriately protective of Fritz but was not aggressive toward Fiona," the Cincinnati Zoo's animal care director, Christina Gorsuch, said at the time. "The exposure was brief but a great first step." Jan 2025: Fiona celebrates her 8th birthday At the beginning of 2025, Fiona celebrated her eighth birthday. Speaking to Fox News Digital, a Cincinnati man said on Friday, "She wasn’t supposed to be here to begin with. The fact that she overcame so much… it was always inspiring. And to see her with her family, you know, mom, dad, half-brother — it was always nice to see." Reflecting on the hippo's early life, Cincinnati Zoo marketing manager Amy LaBarbara said that she was an instant social media hit. "We shared updates on Fiona on social media every day during the first year of her life, and people couldn’t get enough," LaBarbara said at the time. "We even tried to stop at one point but got so much pushback that we kept up with the daily posts." LaBarbara said that "posts about Fiona and her little brother Fritz consistently [got] millions of views and likes from a global audience." Nov 2026: Sudden, shocking loss On Thursday, Nov. 19, Cincinnati Zoo officials announced that Fiona had died after a visitor's hat was tossed in the air and a ceiling fan deflected it over the hippo enclosure's viewing glass. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER "The vet staff tried everything they could to help her after she ingested a hat that ended up in her habitat by accident last week," the statement read. "Despite multiple attempts to move the hat out of her system, it was ultimately too much to overcome," officials added. The zoo said Fiona's team "performed necessary supportive care today in an attempt to save her, but it was not successful and she did not recover." Second lady Usha Vance, a mother of four, paid a heartbreaking tribute to Fiona after the hippo died. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Vance shared a touching family photo of one of her children visiting Fiona as she mourned the death of the world-famous hippo. "We are so sad," she wrote in part on Instagram. Fiona would have been 10 years old in January 2027. "In those 10 years, she inspired millions with her story of survival and did so much to raise awareness and caring for her species," the zoo said. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "She was truly treasured." Zoo officials have asked the public to "keep the people who worked with Fiona and tried to save her in your thoughts and prayers." "They loved her and did their best to save her," the statement added. "They are also, understandably, asking for space at this time." Gorsuch, the director of animal care, said Fritz and the zoo's other hippos, Bibi and Tucker, have been eating and behaving normally since Fiona's death. The area around the Hippo Cove was to be closed throughout the weekend. The animal care team were "shaken and trying to navigate this loss," the zoo said. Our two kids — we have a membership here. And [Fiona] was always a staple of why we came over." Melissa Rudy, Louis Casiano and Bonny Chu, all of Fox News Digital, contributed reporting.

articles.title: US Army to detonate tonnes of unstable explosives in Iowa despite court order
articles.summary: The Army says "swift action" is necessary to protect its personnel and nearby communities around its ammunition plant in Iowa.
articles.body:
The US Army plans to move ahead with detonating five tonnes of degraded explosives in Iowa despite a ruling to halt it indefinitely, a new court filing shows.

"To protect its personnel and the surrounding communities, the Army needs to take swift action," the justice department notified the court on Saturday. "Protection of human health and the environment demand action now, not delay."

The court had ordered a pause after environmental groups sued to stop the detonation, arguing the army failed to consider safer alternatives.

The detonation was originally scheduled for Friday at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown. The army now plans to act by 24 November under an emergency exemption.

In the new filing, the Department of the Army argued that a controlled detonation was necessary to protect the public from an unplanned explosion, a risk it said would become more likely as temperatures were set to fall in the coming days.

"There is an immediate risk that the lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant will explode as temperatures are expected to drop below 30 degrees Fahrenheit (-1C) in the next several days," the filing states.

It argued that the army had removed the doors to the bunker where the barrels were stored in preparation for the detonation and that made the explosives more "vulnerable to temperature changes".

The government has not released details for the rescheduled detonation.

Earlier, the army had warned residents to leave their homes for six hours on the original scheduled day of the explosion, for the duration of the explosion and until the dust settled. An advisory warned "all humans" to avoid being outside in the affected areas while the demolition detonation was set to take place.

Lead azide is a highly volatile compound used as a detonator. Earlier this year, the IAAAP found that the material had degraded over time to the point where it was now too risky to move the material, according to Iowa Public Radio.

On Friday, the military said it was working with the Department of Health and Human Services and the EPA to ensure the explosion was done in the safest manner possible.

Military and environmental officials determined that detonating it in place was the safest way to eliminate the explosive safety hazard.

The EPA, which granted an emergency permit to detonate 68 drums of the material, said it did so because the explosion risk "presented an imminent and substantial threat to human health and the environment".

One of the Environmental groups suing to pause the detonation, the Iowa Environmental Council, argued that many Iowans living within the risk-zone were unaware that the explosion was scheduled to happen.

"There is no safe level of lead exposure, and Iowans were given just days to prepare for the November 20 detonation," the organisation said in a press statement.

The Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club, which filed the lawsuit on Thursday that prompted the court-ordered pause, filed a new motion on Sunday in response to the army's filing.

The group asks the court to pause proceedings so that it may submit additional information before the scheduled detonation.

The motion includes declarations from environmental experts and local officials who support pausing the detonation, citing a lack of public notice and questioning the Army's claim that delay would cause significant risks.

articles.title: Flavio Bolsonaro claims judge ordered passports seized just 7 minutes after Brazil election loss
articles.summary: Former presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro alleges election interference by Brazil’s Supreme Court and discusses political persecution and the future of his family’s political movement.
articles.body: Brazilian Sen. Flavio Bolsonaro accused his country's political and judicial establishment of engineering his presidential election defeat, telling Fox News Digital in an exclusive interview that he fled to the United States amid what he described as a campaign of political persecution — and insisting he lost not to President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, but to "the system." Following a razor-thin election, in which incumbent Lula da Silva won 51.8% to 48.2%, the Brazilian Supreme Court immediately canceled Bolsonaro's passports, prompting the senator and his family to flee the country in dramatic fashion, crossing the border into Argentina and flying into Miami, where President Donald Trump granted them political asylum. Bolsonaro said that he fled for the sake of Brazil, to continue the fight against Alexandre de Moraes and the Brazilian Supreme Court, and alleging both election interference and political persecution. SEN FLAVIO BOLSONARO FLEES BRAZIL FOR US AFTER ELECTION LOSS, WILL BE ISSUED VISAS: STATE DEPARTMENT "I did not leave Brazil to run away. I left for Brazil's sake, and these accusations are completely unfounded. This is a case that began with ‘fake news,’ a false media report, and it's a case that was artificially manufactured against me. "This is the modus operandi, particularly of Alexandre de Moraes in Brazil, when he wants to persecute someone. So, he invented this case against me to leave a kind of sword hanging over my head, something he can use whenever he wants. He wakes up in a bad mood and decides to persecute someone, someone against whom he has artificially manufactured a case," he claimed. "And look, just a few days before the election, he opens this investigation to try to damage my reputation. It's a way for him to interfere in the election to benefit my opponent. And what struck me most was that just seven minutes after the official election results were announced, he took action to seize my passports, to confiscate my passports and prohibit me from leaving the country." Bolsonaro added,"Seven minutes. I emphasize that: just seven minutes after the election ended." He acknowledged he lacks evidence of fraud in the election, but alleged that the electoral system is flawed because it is impossible to demand a recount. "Look, I don't have proof because I'm prohibited from investigating. The elections in Venezuela were also recognized in the past. And everyone knows those elections were fraudulent," he said. "In the most recent elections in Venezuela, it was possible to prove that fraud occurred because they adopted a system that we had been asking Brazil to implement for the 2026 elections." BOLSONARO WINS FIRST ROUND OF BRAZILIAN PRESIDENTIAL ELECTION, AS TRUMP-BACKED CANDIDATES CONTINUE RED WAVE Bolsonaro asked,"What is that system? Electronic voting with an individual printed record of each vote, ensuring the secrecy of the ballot while allowing the votes to be recounted. Let me ask you something: Does Brazil's current system allow votes to be recounted? No," he answered. "What's happening in Brazil is that the technology experts who have been there for years, through several elections, and who are themselves under suspicion, are simply taken at their word. Whatever they say becomes the truth," he claimed. "Nobody has any way to conduct an audit. If we ask for an audit, will it be authorized? No. So, whatever they say becomes the truth. They tell the Superior Electoral Court, the TSE, and the court repeats what they say without even fully understanding whether it's true or not." With Bolsonaro in political exile in the United States, all eyes will turn to Sao Paulo Gov. Tarcisio de Freitas, who cruised to re-election last month, and stepped aside this election cycle to clear the field for Flavio Bolsonaro on the right. Yet election experts disagree with Bolsonaro's assessment over the safety of the nation's voting system. Karina Stange Calandrin, a political scientist and professor at Instituto Brasileiro de Mercado de Capitais (IBMEC), recently told Fox News Digital, "It is an extremely secure and safe system. The machines never connect to the Internet and even the central database system used to transmit tallied votes to TSE must match results issued physically and locally by each individual machine without human interference." Corrupting it, she, would require breaking the seal of each machine and installing software that wouldn’t match the TSE’s version, automatically disqualifying its tally — a scale of collusion so large that it "simply could not pass undetected." BRAZIL’S RAPID ELECTION COUNT PUTS SPOTLIGHT ON VOTING SECURITY AHEAD OF US MIDTERMS While acknowledging the strength of a potential de Freitas candidacy, Bolsonaro is leaving the door open to running in 2030, provided that his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, is still ineligible to run. "Look, thanks to President Bolsonaro, the right in Brazil has many strong leaders with the potential to become president of the republic. Not just Tarcísio de Freitas, but several others." He said, "In a scenario in 2030 where President Jair Bolsonaro is still ineligible to run, I am a candidate. My name is on the table as a candidate for 2030, provided that Congress makes improvements to the electoral system." He continued, "But that is still far in the future. In four years, a lot can happen in politics. With the two years remaining in Donald Trump's presidency, a lot can happen. The political landscape could change completely. So it's still much too early to make those plans." Bolsonaro said "the right has what I call a good problem. Imagine a soccer team with 11-star players ready to take the field. How does the coach decide which player to put in each position? The right has many stars. It has many qualified people, strong candidates capable of running in any election in Brazil." He added, "That's not what happens on the side of evil, on the side of the left, on the side of communism. Over there, the only leader who still exists is the current president of the republic himself, who isn't allowing any prominent figure to emerge as a possible successor." BOLSONARO DECLARES HIMSELF 'LEADER' OF BRAZIL AFTER FLEEING COUNTRY, ARRIVING IN MIAMI Although the 2026 election saw right-wing candidates dominate in the Senate, Chamber of Deputies, and in gubernatorial races, Bolsonaro is calling on his supporters to oppose the re-election of the current speaker of Brazil's lower chamber. "Look, Hugo Motta was never someone from my political camp. He has always been a very pragmatic politician, including in his dealings with left-wing parties." He said, the "problem with Hugo Motta, and the reason I'm advocating against supporting his re-election as president of the Chamber of Deputies, is that two years ago, when he was elected with the support of my party, he promised, for example, to grant amnesty to those being persecuted in Rio de Janeiro. And did he keep that promise? No." He said, "Then they came up with an intermediate proposal, something called ‘dosimetria,’ or sentence recalculation. What is that? It's a new process that doesn't amount to an amnesty at all. It simply reduces, to some extent, the sentences of people who were convicted." He said, "That was approved by the Chamber of Deputies, and the Supreme Federal Court simply suspended it with the stroke of a pen. And whose pen was it? Alexandre de Moraes. So he didn't deliver what he promised." Bolsonaro said the political movement founded by his father is stronger than ever, while maintaining that the United States is the best place for him right now, because he can speak freely, while working with allies in the Brazilian Congress. "The last hope we have is in the National Congress, especially the Federal Senate. Once again, this demonstrates the strength of the right and of the Bolsonaro movement. A lot of people said in the past that they had defeated the Bolsonaro movement… But the results of the 2026 elections, and the votes I officially received, nearly 60 million votes, almost 50% of the valid votes cast for president of Brazil, tell a different story. Look at the number of center-right deputies and senators we helped elect." He noted, "All of this shows that the right and the Bolsonaro movement are stronger than ever. But we're facing a system that is working very hard to prevent Brazil from prospering and to stop the right-wing agenda from advancing." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP He added, "So, as I often say, I didn't lose to my opponent. I lost the election to the system. And that's what makes me so outraged. I'm going to remain here in the United States, continuing to speak out, saying exactly what I think, without holding anything back." He concluded, "I hope not only that God will intervene in our country to save Brazil from communism, but also that our institutions will return to functioning normally." Fox News Digitall's Solly Boussidan and Sydney Finver contributed to this report.

articles.title: California prepares for flooding, rain and wind as Thanksgiving approaches
articles.summary: California officials this weekend are preparing for storms that could coincide with the year’s highest tides, Thanksgiving and some of its busiest holiday travel days.
articles.body: California officials this weekend are preparing for storms that could coincide with the year’s highest tides, Thanksgiving and some of its busiest holiday travel days. “A series of winter storms is impacting California, bringing heavy rain, mountain snow, and potentially hazardous travel conditions,” the California Governor’s Office of Emergency Services said Friday. A Pacific storm is expected to strike the Northern California coast Tuesday and Wednesday, bringing with it an atmospheric river of rain drawn from nearly tropical climes in the ocean, forecasters said. National Weather Service forecasters in the San Francisco Bay Area said the storm would bring “widespread” and persistent rainfall — up to 3 inches in northern portions of the region. A coastal flood warning covering the Bay Area coastline from 6 a.m. Monday to 4 p.m. Thursday said nearly 3 feet of inundation was possible in low-lying areas. Wind gusts of 45 miles per hour are possible in parts of the Bay Area, federal forecasters said. A second storm with atmospheric river precipitation was expected to swing behind the first, the Center for Western Weather and Water Extremes said. There is “considerable disagreement” on timing, location and strength, however, it said in its storm outlook report Friday. Weather service forecasters in the Bay Area said the second storm of the week could arrive late this coming Friday and may affect the weekend. Storm prep underway The Governor’s Office of Emergency Services said the “potential for heavy rainfall and flooding across California” prompted it to move resources, including swift-water rescue teams, to locations around the state where they might be needed. San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie said the city’s emergency operations center was being activated over the weekend to prepare for potential rain- and tide-driven flooding. “We are anticipating high tides and rain that this city has never seen before,” he said on X. “This is extremely serious, and we are acting accordingly at the city level.” He urged people along the water to prepare by stocking up and considering a holiday at home. “I know there’s a lot of travel for many of you as you head into the Thanksgiving holiday, but I’m going to ask you all to consider not traveling unless it is absolutely essential, starting Monday afternoon and into Wednesday,” Lurie said. Perilous king tides The city’s Department of Emergency Management said in a statement that the first of the week’s storms combined with king tides “could result in significant street flooding.” King tides, a term for the highest tides of the year, will come Tuesday through Thursday, the California Coastal Commission said. It set up a series of public meetings to help coastal residents prepare for the worst, including possible flooding. In a Saturday forecast discussion, the weather service’s Bay Area office noted the perils of the week’s first storm: “This system roughly coincides with the first cycle of the King Tides and rain runoff that reaches the Bays to find historically high tide levels may contribute to coastal flooding impacts.” It said the system could also affect travel over the holiday week. Transportation data firm Inrix said the busiest U.S. road travel days ahead of Thanksgiving will be Tuesday and Wednesday. King tides in the Bay Area and beyond could reach 7.5 to 8 feet above the average low tide, the highest in 18 years, according to the U.S. Coast Guard. Water could rise 1 to 2 feet above normal high tides and even more if the high tides take place amid an incoming storm, it said in a statement. “Coastal and low-lying areas around San Francisco Bay, San Pablo Bay, Marin County, San Mateo County, the San Francisco waterfront and ocean beaches are prone to temporary flooding and closures,” the Coast Guard said. Its Sector San Francisco division urged people along the coast to stay away from jetties and rocks and be on the lookout for sneaker waves. Boat owners should make sure their vessels are secure, it said. “Mariners and boaters should inspect mooring lines, dock cleats and waterfront gear ahead of peak tides, as extreme water levels and surges can strain lines or float unsecured items,” the Coast Guard said. California Department of Transportation officials announced the Posey Tube, an East Bay tunnel under the Oakland Estuary that links Alameda Island and Oakland, will be shuttered Sunday through Friday as a precaution. Central Coast could see impacts Along California’s Central Coast, the first of the week’s storms is expected to bring light rain into San Luis Obispo and Santa Barbara counties but is unlikely to bring serious precipitation as far south as urban Los Angeles, federal forecasters there said. A National Weather Service coastal flood advisory, which warns of high surf and tide-driven flooding, is also in place for Catalina and Santa Barbara islands, Santa Barbara County’s southwestern coast and Santa Barbara County’s southeastern coast from early Monday to Thursday afternoon. King tides are also a concern in Southern California, and the Port of San Diego said it’s closing two public access trails along San Diego Bay for the week. Snow in the Sierra Nevadas, storms in Portland The winter pattern storms have origins in the Gulf of Alaska, where low-pressure systems spin in a counterclockwise direction as they sometimes draw precipitation from warmer parts of the Pacific. They often collide with the Pacific Northwest and California and then drive across the continental United States with the help of the eastward jet stream. The Thanksgiving week storms are expected to bring fresh snow to the Sierra Nevada mountain range, the weather service office in Reno, Nevada, said, “bringing periods of difficult travel ... during a very busy holiday travel period.” In Portland, Oregon, there’s a coastal flood watch Monday through Thursday. “A series of systems, coupled with multiple atmospheric rivers will keep widespread precipitation in the forecast through the end of the week,” the weather service said in a forecast discussion. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration last month said “a very strong El Niño” — winter weather influenced by warm waters in the equatorial Pacific — will bring wetter-than-average conditions to California.

articles.title: Australia planted trees across 255 farmland sites to restore habitats; 12 years later, scientists found bird communities moving towards native woodland but still not fully resembling natural habitats after decades
articles.summary: Australia's farmland restoration efforts have helped bird communities move closer to those found in native woodland, but the changes have not been enough
articles.body: Australia's farmland restoration efforts have helped bird communities move closer to those found in native woodland, but the changes have not been enough to restore their original composition. Researchers examined 255 sites in south-west Victoria, comparing farmland, revegetation plantings and areas of remnant native vegetation. The study examined changes recorded over a 12-year period, using bird surveys conducted in 2006/2007 and 2019.According to research published in the journal Ecological Applications, titled ‘Temporal dynamics in the composition of bird communities along a gradient of farmland restoration’, bird communities in restored areas became less similar to those in unrestored farmland and more similar to those in native vegetation. However, the plantings had not fully replicated the bird communities found in natural habitats, even after several decades of growth.How did 12 years of farmland restoration change bird communities in AustraliaThe study covered a heavily cleared agricultural region in south-west Victoria, where more than 90% of the agricultural region had been removed. Researchers selected 23 landscapes, each covering 800 hectares, and surveyed birds across farmland, revegetation plantings and remnant native vegetation. The sites represented different stages of restoration, including plantings aged between 2 and 40 years during the first survey period in 2006/2007.By 2019, those plantings were between 14 and 52 years old. The researchers retained 255 sites for analysis after excluding locations affected by access problems, land-use changes, pine plantations, and wetlands. The sites included 47 native vegetation, 73 revegetation plantings, 63 scattered paddock trees and 75 open pasture, 2 pine plantations, and 16 wetlands/dams.What did bird surveys reveal about Australia's farmland restorationBird surveys took place in 2006/2007 and again in 2019, allowing researchers to examine changes across 12 years. At each site, an observer spent 15 minutes searching a one-hectare area for birds. Every site was surveyed four times, with visits spread across the seasons and divided between mornings and afternoons. Researchers recorded species seen or heard during the surveys and compared the bird communities associated with different habitat types.The analysis considered all land birds as well as woodland birds, which rely on native vegetation for breeding and feeding. Water birds and exotic species were excluded. The researchers assessed changes in community composition, rather than relying only on species numbers.Bird communities in restored Australian farmland moved closer to native woodlandThe results showed that each habitat type supported a distinct bird community. Over the 12 years, bird assemblages in revegetation plantings moved away from those found in unrestored farmland and towards those in remnant native vegetation. The researchers also found that plantings supported richer and more diverse bird assemblages than unrestored farmland.They added a distinct bird community to rural landscapes, increasing the overall diversity of habitats available to birds. The study found that revegetation plantings had not replicated reference habitats even after approximately 40 to 50 years, showing that changes in bird community composition can take much longer.Why did livestock exclusion matter for bird communitiesTwo features of the surrounding landscape and planting management were linked to greater changes in bird communities. Plantings were more likely to move away from the bird assemblages found in unrestored farmland when they were located in areas with greater surrounding tree cover. They were also more likely to show this shift when livestock were mostly excluded, compared with grazed plantings.Complete convergence with reference habitats could take centuries in the study region. Their findings point to the importance of protecting existing natural and semi-natural habitats alongside restoration work. They also have implications for environmental offset programmes, which need to account for the long timescales involved in rebuilding ecological communities.You use AI every day. articles.title: Delta tech issue delays hundreds of flights in and out of Atlanta ahead of Thanksgiving
articles.summary: A problem with the system Delta Air Lines uses to calculate aircraft weight and balance delayed its flights nationwide Sunday as Thanksgiving travel got underway.
articles.body: A problem with the system Delta Air Lines uses to calculate aircraft weight and balance delayed its flights nationwide Sunday as Thanksgiving travel got underway. The Federal Aviation Administration lifted its ground delay program for Atlanta-bound Delta flights at 11:26 a.m. ET, but by 1:55 p.m. ET, 997 flights into and out of Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport had been delayed and 26 had been canceled, according to FlightAware. The FAA briefly halted Atlanta-bound flights Sunday morning, then replaced the ground stop with a program that allowed flights to depart at staggered times. The delay program, requested by Delta, applied to the airline and its regional carriers flying into Hartsfield-Jackson from the contiguous United States. The FAA had projected delays of 57 minutes on average and lasting up to 1 hour and 51 minutes. Delta said it was working to restore the automated system that calculates how much a plane weighs and how that weight is distributed before takeoff. The airline said it was coordinating with air traffic controllers to prevent congestion at gates and on the tarmac in Atlanta. Hartsfield-Jackson said the disruption was limited to Delta and did not affect airport operations broadly. The airport urged travelers to check their flight status with their airline and arrive at least two hours before domestic flights and three hours before international flights. The delays at Hartsfield-Jackson came after the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop on Nov. 13 because of a technical issue with its air traffic control network. Flights resumed later that evening, but travel disruptions continued through the weekend. A separate system outage delayed United Airlines departures on Nov. 16, disrupting crew communications and the airline’s ability to send pilots final aircraft weight data, according to the union representing United pilots. United said it resolved the issue that day.

articles.title: The last home of architect Terry Farrell is on sale for £525,000 inside a historic Kent mansion whose hidden walled garden inspired the 1911 novel The Secret Garden; he lived in one of its apartments from 2009 until his death in 2025
articles.summary: The last home of architect Terry Farrell has hit the market.
articles.body: The last home of architect Terry Farrell has hit the market. The historic house is up for sale with an asking price of £525,000, according to a report by Country Life. His apartment sits inside Great Maytham Hall, a Grade II listed mansion near Rolvenden in Kent, redesigned by architect Edwin Lutyens for the Tennant family between 1909 and 1912. Farrell moved into the first-floor apartment, known as the Burnett Suite, in 2009 and lived there until his death in September 2025, aged 87. The property is being marketed by Charlotte Day.The mansion also has another claim to fame. It was the home of children's author Frances Hodgson Burnett, who rented the property between 1898 and 1907. During her stay, she discovered a walled garden hidden behind thick ivy. A robin is said to have led her to the garden, which she later restored with rose bushes and turned into a place to write. The garden became her inspiration for her 1911 novel The Secret Garden.Lutyens kept the garden, changed the houseGreat Maytham Hall dates back to 1721, although much of the original building was destroyed by a fire in 1893. Only its two 18th-century wings remain standing. In 1909, Harold Tennant, a Liberal politician who later served as Secretary of State for Scotland under his brother-in-law, H. H. Asquith, bought the estate. He hired Edwin Lutyens to rebuild the house. Lutyens, who is known for his country houses in the Arts and Crafts style, had to try something different here. After all, this house demanded grandeur. The new house was given a Palladian character. It was almost like a miniature Blenheim Palace. While Lutyens changed the house, he made sure to keep the walled garden. He worked with garden designer Gertrude Jekyll on the new layout.The Tennant family lived there until the Second World War, when the army requisitioned the property. During the war, the grounds served a rather practical purpose: the roses gave way to cabbages and leeks, and the lawns were dug up for potatoes. A bomb later fell on the estate. It missed the main house but destroyed the greenhouses and part of the garden. Over the years, the hall deteriorated. In 1965, a country house charity bought and restored it. The building was then divided into the apartments you see today.Farrell’s tribute roomsTerry Farrell, the architect behind London’s MI6 building at Vauxhall Cross, was fascinated by the house’s past. While living there, he refreshed three ground-floor rooms and hung around 70 pictures on the walls. Most showed Lutyens’s work. The rest were portraits of people who shaped the hall, including Burnett, Tennant and Tennant’s sister, Margot, who married Asquith. He eventually gave the pictures to the Lutyens Trust, which has loaned them back to the building permanently.“Living here at Great Maytham Hall, I take great pleasure in walking about and studying the underlying geometrical organisations that are the foundations of Lutyens’s great work here. The grandest of these is the overall site masterplan, which is focused on some very clear primary principles. The key one is that the main linear block is strung along an east-west line that is very deliberately placed all along a gentle topographical edge, thereby dividing all the land and the garden experiences into two distinct zones,” Farrell said in a statement published on the trust’s website. Though the home has changed hands, it still tells the architect’s story.Inside the Burnett SuiteThe apartment sits on the first floor and can be reached by lift or via the grand communal staircase. One of its highlights is the sitting room, which has high ceilings. “The property benefits from an impressive entertaining sitting room, with 3.25m ceiling heights and multiple windows giving lovely views across the extensive grounds,” the listing describes. There is a feature fireplace and a study that overlooks the rear terraces. The home also has a separate kitchen and one double bedroom. The Energy Performance Certificate is currently rated D, with the potential to reach C. Anyone buying the property would need to plan for that upgrade. The ivy-covered walls are still there, and so is the garden.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? Build Your Legacy with TOI Homes.

articles.title: FAA lifts ground stop on Atlanta-bound Delta flights after system outage
articles.summary: Delta Air Lines says crews are using manual workarounds after an outage in its weight-and-balance system reportedly delayed at least 3,500 flights.
articles.body: A Sunday morning outage in Delta Air Lines' automated weight-and-balance system forced the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to briefly halt Atlanta-bound flights and has reportedly delayed at least 3,500 Delta flights across major hubs, including Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport and New York's LaGuardia Airport. The technical failure rippled through Sunday's travel schedule, but the ground stop led to roughly an hour delay before being lifted. "Delta teams are using manual workarounds this morning to safely get flights departed while work continues to restore automation," Delta told Fox News in a statement. "We thank our customers for their patience and our people for their professionalism." UNITED AIRLINES SAYS TECHNOLOGY ISSUE RESOLVED AFTER ‘WIDESPREAD SYSTEM OUTAGE’ The FAA stressed the outage was specific to Delta and "not related" to air traffic control systems. "Delta is working to resolve issues with the airline’s weight and balance automation system," FAA wrote Sunday on X. "These delays are not related to any FAA air traffic systems. Please check with Delta for the latest information." Before any commercial aircraft can take off, crews must verify that its total weight and center of gravity fall within strict safety limits – a process that relies heavily on baggage and cargo data. With the automated system offline, Delta staff were calculating weight and balance figures manually for departing flights while technicians work to bring the software back online. DUFFY: INVESTIGATORS EXAMINING 2 ROUTERS AFTER NATIONWIDE FAA GROUND STOP, NO SIGNS OF FOREIGN CYBERATTACK The airline coordinated with air traffic controllers to manage the flow of planes and prevent congestion at airport gates and on the tarmac at its Atlanta hub. A ground delay for Atlanta had remained in effect for Delta only after the ground stop had been lifted, the airport said in a statement. "Hartsfield-Jackson is aware of operational issues affecting Delta flights at ATL. Based on our latest information, the ground delay applies to Delta departures only. It is not airportwide," the statement said. "Delta is managing the issue with its operations team." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The issue comes more than a week after a historic nationwide FAA ground stop and an ensuing week of ongoing cybersecurity issues from reported system upgrades and patches throughout the U.S. The issues caused panic online that percolated into the stock market, causing massive dips in tech and artificial intelligence stocks. Fox News' C.B. Cotton contributed to this report.

articles.title: A Texas woman blocked a neighbour online after repeated unwanted visits; he later hurled rocks through her windows and caused an estimated $4,400 in damage, and a November 2026 court upheld his two-year jail term
articles.summary: A Texas appeals court has upheld the two-year state jail sentence of a man convicted of damaging his neighbour's home by throwing rocks at it, rejecting
articles.body: A Texas appeals court has upheld the two-year state jail sentence of a man convicted of damaging his neighbour's home by throwing rocks at it, rejecting his arguments that prosecutors failed to establish the extent of the financial loss.The Fourth Court of Appeals in San Antonio affirmed the conviction of Alberto Ruben Hernandez in a ruling delivered on November 18, 2026. Hernandez was convicted of criminal mischief causing property damage worth at least $2,500 but less than $30,000.The case dates back to September 8, 2022, when Hernandez's neighbour, Misty Martin, was at work. Another neighbour, Jay Saunders, heard shouting, cursing and breaking glass coming from Martin's property. He looked outside and saw Hernandez throwing rocks at her house.When Hernandez noticed Saunders watching him, he allegedly told him to stay out of his business before approaching his house and throwing a rock through one of its windows. Saunders's wife, Jessica Delarosa, called 911.When Martin returned home, she found several broken windows, damaged door and window frames and a hole in an interior wall after a rock had passed through a bedroom window.Contractor estimated repair costs at $4,400Martin approached local contractor Garrett Bounds for an estimate to repair the damage. Based on photographs of the property, Bounds prepared an itemised estimate of $4,400.The estimate included $1,200 for replacement windows, $2,000 for labour, $200 for additional materials and $1,000 for painting.Hernandez challenged the estimate during his appeal, arguing that Bounds had not personally inspected the property, taken measurements or checked the prices of replacement materials. He also questioned why the estimate included four replacement windows when Martin had testified that three were broken.However, the appeals court said Bounds had extensive construction experience and had owned his construction business since 2006. It ruled that the limitations in his estimation method concerned the weight of his testimony, not whether it was sufficient evidence.The court also noted that the law measures financial loss by the reasonable cost of repairing or restoring damaged property, not simply the amount the owner eventually spends.Court rejects other arguments against convictionHernandez also challenged photographs showing damage to his neighbours' property, arguing that the images were unrelated to the charges against him.The court rejected the argument, saying the damage occurred during the same incident and the photographs supported the eyewitness accounts identifying Hernandez.He further argued that prosecutors' use of the word "victim" to describe Martin undermined his presumption of innocence. However, the judges said he had not objected to the references during the trial and had therefore failed to preserve the issue for appeal.The appeals court rejected all three challenges and upheld the original conviction and two-year sentence.You use AI every day. articles.title: A California drone operator filming sharks from nearly two miles away spotted a large great white approaching a fisherman who had jumped into the water; he used the drone to warn the man, who climbed back aboard
articles.summary: A quiet day off the California coast nearly turned into a dangerous encounter when a fisherman enjoying a swim beside his boat unknowingly entered the
articles.body: A quiet day off the California coast nearly turned into a dangerous encounter when a fisherman enjoying a swim beside his boat unknowingly entered the path of a large great white shark. While the man remained unaware of the predator approaching beneath the surface, a filmmaker watching from a beach nearly two miles away spotted the danger through his drone camera. Quick thinking and an aerial warning helped the fisherman return safely to his boat before the encounter could take a potentially disastrous turn.Drone filmmaker spots shark approaching fishermanAccording to Surfer, the incident was captured by Carlos Gauna, a California-based filmmaker and wildlife enthusiast widely known as The Malibu Artist for his aerial footage of sharks along the coastline.Gauna was operating his drone from a beach nearly two miles away when he noticed a large juvenile great white shark swimming close to a fishing boat. The shark was estimated to measure between 10 and 11 feet.A fisherman had jumped into the water beside the vessel, apparently unaware of the animal's presence. Two live fish were hanging from a stringer attached to the boat, creating an additional attraction for the predator.Knowing the shark was dangerous, Gauna used his drone to warn the fisherman. The man climbed back on the ship to avoid the animal.Whiskey Riff also reported the encounter, highlighting how drone technology can provide an important safety advantage when people are unaware of marine wildlife nearby.Live fish may have attracted the great whiteThe presence of the two fish was an important detail in the incident. According to Gauna's observations, struggling fish can release signals that attract sharks searching for potential food.Surfer said the incident showed why ocean awareness is crucial for swimsuits near fishing boats. Although the fisherman was not deliberately attracting sharks, keeping a fresh catch hanging in the water could increase the likelihood of attracting predators.Great white sharks sense prey. Their ability to detect vibrations and chemical signals in the water makes struggling fish particularly noticeable.Whiskey Riff says sharks may snack on unfamiliar objects. Although humans are not their natural prey, an unexpected encounter with a large shark can still carry serious risks.Not all shark sightings are attacksVideo is scary, but episode was not an attack. The surfer could distinguish between a shark swimming near people and one trying to attack.Research by Dr Chris Lowe, director of California State University's Shark Lab, has also indicated that juvenile white sharks frequently swim near people without biting.The presence of a shark therefore does not automatically mean an attack is imminent. However, its size and proximity, combined with the presence of struggling fish, made the fisherman's situation worth taking seriously.Drone footage highlights importance of ocean awarenessGauna's footage is part of his broader work documenting great white sharks along California's coastline. His recordings frequently capture sharks moving near surfers, swimmers and fishing vessels, sometimes without the people involved noticing them.According to Whiskey Riff, the incident demonstrated how aerial technology can help identify potential dangers that remain difficult to see from water level.Image Courtesy: SurferYou use AI every day. articles.title: Russian vessel hit by suspected Ukrainian drone at Libya’s Benghazi port
articles.summary: There was no immediate reaction from Russia, and no one has claimed responsibility for the suspected attack.
articles.body:
A suspected sea drone attack has hit a Russian vessel in eastern Libya, causing an explosion and a brief fire, according to the North African country’s eastern-based government.

Local sources told Al Jazeera late on Sunday that an unknown number of Libyan and Russian nationals were killed in the attack at dawn, adding that the ship was moored inside the civil sea port of Benghazi, close to a naval base.

The sources said the ship was carrying weapons, ammunition and drones in its cargo. Local sources quoted residents as saying that they saw three drones attack the vessel.

Satellite imagery provider Vantor said imagery showed the vessel was the Merkury, a Russian Navy corvette, or small warship.

Imagery taken on Sunday showed that most of the vessel ‌had capsized and sunk, with only its bow still visible above water. Smoke was also visible rising from part of the ship’s superstructure, with significant debris scattered along the pier.

The Benghazi-based administration earlier said the vessel had docked to refuel and take on supplies under a cooperation agreement between Russia and Libya’s eastern government.

Late on Sunday, the AP news agency quoted unnamed sources as saying that several Ukrainian sea drones were launched at the ship from a base run by Ukrainian forces in western Libya.

Also on Sunday evening, another sea drone hit a Malta-flagged commercial vessel off the port of Benghazi in a separate attack. The Benghazi-administration’s Health Ministry said all crew members “who were injured when a merchant vessel was targeted this evening by explosives-laden sea drones off the coast of Benghazi” had been rescued and were receiving treatment.

No further details were given. The Almasar satellite television channel said that naval and air forces destroyed at least 12 other sea drones off the Mediterranean city.

The Benghazi-based administration said it had launched a joint investigation with Russia to “uncover the circumstances of the attack, its source, and the party behind it”.

The government said the fire had been brought under control and the site secured, while it condemned the suspected strike as a violation of Libya’s sovereignty and a threat to maritime safety.

“The Libyan government will not allow Libyan ports, territory or territorial waters to be turned into an arena for settling scores or exporting international conflicts,” it said, adding that Libya was “not a party to the Russian-Ukrainian war”.

Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Ukrainian forces have repeatedly used naval drones and missiles to target Russian warships and naval facilities in the Black Sea.

On Saturday, a drone struck a Russian cargo ship in the eastern Baltic Sea near Finnish waters. Finland’s border guard attributed the strike to Ukraine.

A Russian liquefied natural gas carrier sank off the Libyan coast in March after an attack that Russian President Vladimir Putin blamed on Ukraine, while last December, Ukraine said it had used aerial drones to strike a Russian-linked oil tanker in the Mediterranean.

Libya has been divided since a NATO-backed uprising toppled longtime leader Muammar Gaddafi, who was later killed, in 2011.

A United Nations-recognised government is based in Tripoli and a rival administration is in the east. The oil-rich nation remains a focal point for a long-running rivalry between Russia and the West.

articles.title: 'We do need answers': Trump aide Bessent on Nvidia's sale of chips to China
articles.summary: US treasury secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday said the Trump administration was seeking answers from Nvidia over its chip sales to China and wanted to
articles.body: US treasury secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday said the Trump administration was seeking answers from Nvidia over its chip sales to China and wanted to establish who was responsible for compliance at the company following the resignation of its former chief executive, Jensen Huang.Bessent said the administration had been in touch with Nvidia's interim management, board members and legal team but was yet to receive answers about the company's compliance practices and how much of its management was aware of the reported issues."We've been in touch with the temporary management, with the lead directors, with their lawyers, and we do need answers.... It behooves Nvidia to move quickly on this because we want to know what the culture was," Bessent told CBS' "Face the Nation"."We do need to see who was in charge of compliance there," Bessent said. "We will see which level of the business knew about this. Was it at the lower levels? Was it at the middle level? Did it go all the way to the top?" he added.Bessent stated that the US administration did not yet have answers about Nvidia's chip sales to China and expected the company to provide clarity.He further expressed confidence that the company's board would conduct a thorough review and provide answers.US President Donald Trump on Friday said he would like to see Huang apologise and return to Nvidia. Asked whether he supported the idea, Bessent said more information was needed before taking a position."I think we have to see where the buck stops," he added.Nvidia board chairman Harvey Jones has said the company would not rehire Huang.Earlier last week, Bessent had called for Nvidia to look outside the company while choosing its next chief executive, arguing that the reported developments pointed to the need for a major change in its internal culture."This makes me think that as the board conducts a search for a new leader that they need to go outside the company, that just (with) what was going on inside the company, they need a dramatic shakeup," Bessent told Fox News' "Sunday Morning Futures".He also said Nvidia's board and external legal advisers should address questions about the company's compliance culture and adherence to US export restrictions within the next 10 days.Huang's resignation followed reports about his alleged relationships, including an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, a former senior executive at Megaspeed International, an Nvidia customer. US intelligence reportedly suspects her of being involved in espionage for China.The reports triggered investigations by US regulators and the FBI, congressional action, an internal company review and a proposed investor class-action lawsuit.Days after Huang's resignation, the Trump administration issued a rule further restricting China's access to advanced artificial intelligence (AI) chips manufactured by companies such as Nvidia.The move tightened export controls ahead of Trump's visit to China last week for talks with President Xi Jinping.On November 10, Nvidia's independent board members appointed the Wall Street law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct an independent investigation.The decision followed reports by The New York Times and The Wall Street Journal about Huang's alleged relationships and US authorities' suspicions regarding Alice Huang.You use AI every day. articles.title: COP31 climate talks fail to reach deal amid fossil fuel and money rows
articles.summary: The talks fail to make a breakthrough on tackling climate change after a row about mentioning fossil fuels.
articles.body:
Countries have failed to reach a major new deal to tackle climate change after deep divisions over fossil fuels and money emerged at the UN COP31 talks in Turkey.

Negotiations were due to finish on Friday but ran late into Sunday in search of common ground, becoming the longest UN climate conference in history.

But the final deal proved unacceptable to the EU, Pacific island nations and others because it failed to directly mention fossil fuels, the main cause of global warming.

Meanwhile, many poorer countries objected to the absence of any clear financial commitments from richer nations to help them adapt to the impacts of rising temperatures.

The last time a COP's main political agreement collapsed like this was in 2009 in Copenhagen.

UN secretary general Antonio Guterres, in his last COP before he steps down, said he was "deeply disappointed".

He took aim at what he called "powerful fossil fuel interests" who he said were taking "a page from Big Tobacco's playbook: distorting the science, delaying policy, blocking action, and piling up huge profits while people everywhere pay the price".

After two weeks of negotiations, exhausted delegates were presented with a new, draft deal in the early hours of Sunday morning to try to break the deadlock.

But the words "fossil fuels" did not appear anywhere in the text. The only indirect reference to coal, oil and gas was a nod to a deal agreed at COP28 in 2023 , when countries agreed to "transition away" from fossil fuels in energy systems.

The EU's representative, Irish Minister Darragh O'Brien, made it clear that the EU "strongly" objected, saying that the "decisions go nowhere near the level of ambition needed to tackle climate change".

"It is unconscionable that we would have a climate pact that makes no mention of fossil fuels," he said.

Other countries, such as Panama and the Marshall Islands, also criticised the deal for doing nowhere near enough to tackle the pace of climate change.

A first draft of the deal on Monday mentioned "fossil fuel" or "fossil fuels" six times, but that was unacceptable to oil-producing nations.

Saudi Arabia's delegate Mohammad Ayoub said that Arab countries "continued to engage in good faith" but argued that they only accounted for a small proportion of historical greenhouse gas emissions.

Russia warned not to "turn to slogans" over coal, oil and gas, claiming that if countries moved away from fossil fuels too quickly it would lead to "fuel poverty".

Another major sticking point has been money for poorer countries to adapt to the impacts of climate change, such as more intense heatwaves and more severe droughts.

Last year at COP30 in Brazil , nations agreed to triple the finance for that purpose.

But this year's deal contained no reference to concrete figures, nor the baseline against which that pledge would be measured. This raised fears it would give richer nations too much wriggle room.

"Rich nations and polluting governments cannot keep arriving empty-handed," said Mohamed Adow of Power Shift Africa, an African climate and energy think tank.

The UK's Energy Secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, described the failure to reach a political agreement as "immensely disappointing".

"This only strengthens our resolve to work with partners around the world on the genuine progress made in Antalya on tackling the climate crisis," she said, adding that the UK's commitment was "unwavering".

While talks were hosted in Antalya in Turkey, Australia led the official negotiations - creating what some observers described as a chaotic dynamic.

Chris Bowen, Australian government minister and COP31 president of negotiations, said that there were "unbridgeable red lines" in the discussions.

He pointed to "the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory". At the same time, "the impacts of climate change are getting worse", he said, raising the stakes.

The year 2026 could end as the hottest on record and has brought extreme weather and natural hazards to much of the world, from summer heat and drought in Europe to flash flooding in Nepal .

And COP31 was the first annual UN conference to formally discuss how one of the key international targets for limiting climate change would be missed.

In the Paris talks of 2015 , nearly 200 countries agreed to try to limit global warming to 1.5C above pre-industrial levels of the late 1800s, aimed at avoiding some of the worst effects of climate change.

The UN says that the Paris deal has driven "near-universal" climate action. In the early 2010s, global warming of 4C or more was thought to be a serious possibility by the end of the century.

Now, the world is likely to limit warming to about 2.8C by 2100 based on current government policies, the UN says.

But action has not been fast enough to meet that Paris goal, with the world likely to "overshoot" 1.5C of long-term warming in the next few years.

Many countries say they are committed to eventually bringing warming back down to 1.5C, but that will require an ambitious ramping up of technologies - which do not yet exist at scale - to remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.

Although the main deal fell through, some agreements were reached, including progress on a "just transition mechanism" - a framework to support workers and communities as economies shift towards clean energy.

The COP31 president also said that more than 80 countries backed Turkey's target to increase the share of global energy use met by electricity to 35% by 2035

But following today's events, some have questioned whether the UN climate process - which relies on consensus - can succeed in a geopolitically divided world.

The UN's climate chief, Simon Stiell, said he would seek advice on potential reform to the process, with the next conference scheduled for November 2027, COP32 in Ethiopia.

"[The consensus process] has worked to get us where we are," he told the BBC. "It got us through Paris... so it can work," but acknowledged it "fell short" today.

The UN climate process has "suffered setback before and come back stronger," Stiell told delegates. "It must do so again."

articles.title: A San Francisco mansion sold for $21 million in June 2026; just five months later, the same five-bedroom Presidio Heights property has sold again for $24 million after a minor makeover
articles.summary: A five-bedroom mansion in San Francisco’s Presidio Heights has found a buyer.
articles.body: A five-bedroom mansion in San Francisco’s Presidio Heights has found a buyer. The property at 3501 Jackson Street sold for $24 million, according to a report by The Real Deal. This is the second time the house has changed hands. The seller bought the home in June for $21 million. The latest sale represents a $3 million increase in value over that period.Presidio Heights mansion sold for the second timeThe property at 3501 Jackson Street is roughly 8,000 square feet across four levels. It first hit the market earlier this year. It first sold off-market in June for $21 million before returning to the market on November 6.Nina Hatvany, the Compass agent who represented both parties and co-listed the home with Paul Kitchen, told The San Francisco Standard that a house the owner had wanted for years had become available, and the owner had to act. The seller, whose identity is concealed behind an LLC, had been eyeing the other property for about 15 years, according to Hatvany. When it came up, the decision was quick.The home hit the market on November 6 with an asking price of $19.9 million. The seller accepted a bid on November 9. According to Hatvany, in competitive markets such as this, people do not sit on it before making decisions. "You see this particularly with the more expensive and unique properties, where basically somebody just has to have the property, and they have the resources to make that happen," she told the outlet. The deal closed earlier this week at $24 million. This amounts to about $2,990 per square foot, compared with roughly $2,620 in June. That is a $3 million increase in just a few months. "The market has gone up for luxury properties very significantly in the last few months in San Francisco. It's just exploded… and prices for unique properties have really escalated," the listing agent told the outlet.Hatvany told the local outlet that the June buyers paid transfer taxes and commissions, which put their all-in cost near $22 million. Four more bedrooms sit on the other floors, so no one has to share a hallway with a guest. The ground floor opens into a living room big enough for a ballroom, with arched doorways. Beside it are a formal dining room and a library. At the back, a chef’s kitchen flows into a family room. French doors run along the main floor and open onto limestone terraces, a fountain courtyard and a raised dining pavilion, so the party can spill outside without anyone leaving the house.Downstairs, there is a home theatre and a refrigerated wine cellar, all curated for grand entertaining. An elevator connects every level. The 1922 millwork and mouldings were retained during the renovation, so the craftsmanship of the original house is still visible in every room. A two-car garage with side-by-side parking provides ample space for vehicles. No wonder a home like this found buyers twice this year.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: ‘Horrific’ and ‘chilling’: Officials condemn ICE arrests at Seattle airport
articles.summary: Video shows masked immigration agents forcibly detaining two people at Seattle airport, raising concerns over tactics.
articles.body:
Democrats and state officials have denounced a now-viral immigration arrest in Washington state, which took place on an airport jet bridge as passengers were boarding a flight to Los Angeles.

“What we’ve seen happening in Washington is atrocious,” said Nevada’s Governor-elect Aaron Ford, a Democrat, in an interview with the news outlet MS NOW on Sunday.

He added that he supported safeguards to restrict the actions taken by United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents.

“ We need some control over these vigilante ICE agents who come en masse in terrorising neighbourhoods, at airports included,” Ford said.

The two arrests unfolded on Saturday morning at Seattle-Tacoma international airport, as passengers boarded Alaska Airlines Flight 1306.

Videos recorded by passengers showed immigration agents in masks surrounding a man and a woman on the narrow jet bridge, forcing them to the ground as other travellers looked on.

Passengers could be heard asking the officers to identify themselves, while a woman repeatedly shouted that she and her family had work permits.

In one video, a young girl can be heard screaming as officers remove a man through a side door. In another part of the footage, an officer appeared to shove a bystander who tried to intervene.

The flight was delayed, eventually departing about three hours later than expected.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) defended the operation, saying ICE had conducted a targeted enforcement action to arrest Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, a Mexican national who the agency said had overstayed his visa.

DHS alleged that other travellers began obstructing and assaulting officers during the arrest, including one passenger who allegedly “hurled hot coffee on the officers”.

The woman who was arrested, identified as Sofia Hernandez Mejia, was also found to have overstayed her visa, the department said, adding that she would be charged with assaulting a federal officer.

The agency did not say where the two were taken.

The footage prompted sharp condemnation from Washington Governor Bob Ferguson, who called ICE “completely and totally out of control” and described the video as “horrific” and “chilling” at a news conference on Saturday.

Ferguson also questioned whether the agents violated a Washington state law he signed in March that restricts law enforcement officers from wearing facial coverings.

“Masked agents who do not identify themselves drag screaming individuals off a jetway as they’re about to do something very ordinary in our country: board a flight. There is no justification for this brutality,” Ferguson said during the news conference.

He added that state officials were investigating the circumstances of the arrests, including how the agents accessed the jet bridge.

Ferguson also urged Alaska Airlines and other carriers to demand that federal immigration agents leave airports.

Alaska Airlines said it did not receive advance notice of the enforcement operation and was working with Ferguson and the Port of Seattle to determine whether established protocols had been followed.

The Port of Seattle, which manages the airport, said in a statement that it has raised its concerns with the relevant federal authorities about whether regulations were breached.

At Saturday’s news conference, Port of Seattle Commissioner Hamdi Mohamed characterised the arrests as particularly distressing because of when they took place.

“We are entering the holidays. That is one of the most heartbreaking things about this moment today. There are so many people in that airport that are travelling to go and connect with their families,” Mohamed said. “And that family is separated.”

Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson also condemned the operation, describing the agents’ tactics as “unacceptable and un-American”.

Protesters gathered at the airport on Saturday evening, in the hours after the confrontation, to condemn the arrests and call for accountability from federal authorities.

Disapproval of Trump’s immigration crackdown

The arrests come as President Donald Trump continues to pursue what he has promised will be the largest deportation effort in US history.

But voters have expressed concern about the tactics used during his immigration crackdown. Some experts believe the topic became a political liability for Republicans in the November 3 midterm elections.

A Fox News poll from September found that 53 percent of registered voters believed the administration’s immigration enforcement had gone too far . The figure rose to 60 percent among independent voters and two-thirds of Hispanic respondents.

In a November 8 interview with the CBS News television programme 60 Minutes, Trump acknowledged that his administration’s deportation policies may have been too aggressive, saying, “I think it might be too tough, yeah.”

In the midterms, the Democratic Party won majorities in both the US House of Representatives and the Senate, flipping both chambers from Republican control.

In the wake of that victory, several high-profile members of the left-wing party have pledged to seek reforms to immigration enforcement operations in the US.

Senators Alex Padilla and Jacky Rosen, for instance, have introduced legislation that would prevent ICE from carrying out arrests at or near airports without a judicial warrant first.

Patty Murray, another Democratic senator, also said she was demanding answers from DHS and warned in a post on X that the administration would face consequences when the incoming Congress is sworn in early next year.

“Trump answers to a Democratic Congress on January 3rd – there WILL be accountability,” she wrote.

articles.title: An Ohio stepson used his stepmother's trust to buy Colorado land and a $154,000 car for himself, then sought control of her affairs; an appeals court rejected his latest bid to reopen the guardianship ruling
articles.summary: A family member entrusted with the finances of an elderly woman was at the center of a legal dispute after questions were raised about how her money was
articles.body: A family member entrusted with the finances of an elderly woman was at the center of a legal dispute after questions were raised about how her money was being spent. An Ohio man sought to take control of his stepmother’s personal and financial matters after using her trust funds to buy and sell property and to purchase an expensive luxury automobile. But after losing his original custody battle, an appeals court also rejected his latest attempt to reopen the case.Appeals court tosses latest legal challengeThe First District Ohio Court of Appeals said Kristian Guntzelman, stepson of Dixie Foust, did not show cause to reopen the guardianship proceedings. In a decision dated November 20, 2026, the appellate court upheld the Hamilton County Probate Court’s denial of the request to reconsider its earlier decision.Guntzelman filed a motion for relief from the original decision pursuant to Ohio Civil Rule 60(B). He contended that other financial documents should have been taken into account and that the probate court should have held an evidentiary hearing before denying his request.The appeals court said he had not provided any legally sufficient reason to overturn the previous ruling or prove he had a potentially successful claim.Trust fund transactions for property and luxury carsThe dispute arose from Guntzelman’s position as an agent acting under Foust’s 2020 durable power of attorney, granting him access to her financial resources.In 2024, during guardianship proceedings, evidence was brought before the magistrate of several questionable transactions involving her trust. The Ohio Court of Appeals said Guntzelman used trust money in connection with the purchase of two large parcels of land in Cascade, Colorado.One property was described as a home Guntzelman and his wife would build on, the other as an investment for the trust. He said he had taken out a short-term loan to facilitate a swift transaction.Investigators also looked into his purchase of a $154,000 Lucid Motors luxury electric vehicle with trust assets. The car was payment for taking care of his stepmother's financial matters, Guntzelman said.But the magistrate questioned the logic behind the payment, saying the proposed annual compensation of between $15,000 and $19,000 was well below the price of the vehicle.Guardianship refused over concerns about financial judgmentFoust’s personal and estate guardianship was filed for by Guntzelman in April 2024. Her brother, Randy Foust, filed a competing application shortly thereafter.Witnesses at hearings in July and August 2024 raised concerns about the management of her money. Ultimately, the magistrate denied Guntzelman’s application Aug. 20, citing questionable financial transactions and concerns about his ability to responsibly manage her assets.Then the probate court appointed independent guardians to oversee the personal welfare and estate of Foust. Guntzelman appealed the decision but the denial was upheld in a separate ruling by the Ohio Court of Appeals in 2025.Judges explain why new evidence fell shortIn his most recent plea, Guntzelman said records of the financial transactions could prove his actions were legitimate. However, the Ohio Court of Appeals determined that some of these records predated the initial guardianship decision and could have been presented at an earlier time.The judges also noted that the original written objections he had filed against the magistrate’s findings had been based on legal arguments and not the disputed financial transactions.The court also found his request didn’t satisfy the requirements for relief under Ohio civil rule 60(B), which allows judgments to be reviewed under certain circumstances. His application also had been submitted after the one-year time limit that applied to some grounds for relief.Importantly, the appellate judges said that even if the documents indicated the deals were legal, that did not necessarily change the outcome. The main question was whether Guntzelman exercised reasonable care in dealing with his stepmother’s money, considering the risky investments and the large purchase of the car.What's moreAccordingly, the November 20, 2026 decision in In re Guardianship of Foust affirmed the probate court's denial of a motion to reopen the proceeding or to hold another evidentiary hearing.The ruling leaves intact the independent guardianship arrangement and ends Guntzelman’s latest attempt to have the decision refusing him control over his stepmother’s affairs overturned.Image Courtesy: Google GeminiYou use AI every day. articles.title: Natural gas pipeline fire shoots flames into the air in Alabama, cause is under investigation
articles.summary: WARD, Ala. — A fire on a natural gas pipeline lit up the night sky in rural Alabama late Saturday with a towering column of orange flame, prompting the operator to shut down part of the line but causing no injuries, the company said.
articles.body: WARD, Ala. — A fire on a natural gas pipeline lit up the night sky in rural Alabama late Saturday with a towering column of orange flame, prompting the operator to shut down part of the line but causing no injuries, the company said. The cause of the fire is under investigation and customer deliveries were not impacted, Southern Natural Gas Company said in a statement Sunday. Photos and videos posted on social media appeared to show flames rising dozens of yards above the trees near Ward, with smoke billowing into the air. People said on social media that the fire was visible from miles away across the state line in Mississippi. Southern Natural Gas said it “experienced a natural gas release and fire” on the segment of the pipeline at around 11:30 p.m. CST Saturday. Emergency responders and company personnel secured the area and the blaze was extinguished, the company said. The impacted part of the pipeline was shut down and depressurized. The Sumter County Emergency Management Agency did not immediately respond to a voicemail seeking information.
