articles.title: Kaiga nuclear unit-1 attains criticality again, gets a second life
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: In a big milestone for the country’s nuclear sector, Kaiga Generating Station Unit-1 (KGS-1) in Karnataka successfully attained criticality
articles.body: NEW DELHI: In a big milestone for the country’s nuclear sector, Kaiga Generating Station Unit-1 (KGS-1) in Karnataka successfully attained criticality early Sunday for the second time, giving a new lease of life to the nuclear power unit that had been taken offline for life-extension work after 25 years of operation. The disclosure was made on Sunday by Nuclear Power Corporation of India Limited (NPCIL), the PSU that designs, builds, commissions and operates nuclear power plants across India.A unit attaining criticality means it has reached a self-sustaining, controlled nuclear fission chain reaction inside its reactor core.KGS-1 had reached first criticality on Sept 26, 2000, and had supplied 37,670 million units before it was shut down for refurbishment activities in April last year. The same unit had set a world record for 962 days of continuous operation on Dec 31, 2018, operating at a 99.3% plant load factor, surpassing the previous global record of 940 days held by Heysham II (Unit 8/Reactor 2) in the UK.“The accomplishing this in just 600 days following its shutdown for major refurbishment activities of EMCCR (en-masse coolant channel replacement) and EMFR (en-masse feeder replacement) on April 1, 2025, KGS-1 has set a new fleet-wide benchmark as the first NPCIL reactor to reach criticality in such a short span,” NPCIL said on X on Sunday. It said, “This remarkable success stands as a reflection of extraordinary dedication, technical excellence, and unified teamwork.”Kaiga generating station has four operational nuclear units totalling 880 MW and two additional units (5 and 6) under construction, adding 1,400 MW and bringing the total planned capacity to 2,280 MW across six units.Kaiga Units-5 & 6 are state-of-the-art, indigenous 700 MW pressurized heavy-water reactors (PHWRs), which incorporate advanced safety features and are among the safest in the world. Three such PHWRs — KAPS-3&4 and RAPP-7 — are successfully operating in the states of Gujarat and Rajasthan respectively. The components and equipment for the project are supplied by domestic industry partners and works are being executed by Indian contractors, aligning with the Atmanirbhar initiatives of the Modi govt.Just days before, in another development, Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB) granted permission for the first approach to criticality of Rajasthan atomic power project unit-8 (RAPP-8) at Rawatbhata, following satisfactory completion of safety reviews.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Missouri mom charged with murder after police say 3-year-old died of untreated cancer
articles.summary: A Missouri mother and another caretaker have been charged with murder in the death of her emaciated 3-year-old son, who died from cancer in a squalid, roach-infested home two years after doctors found a tumor on his adrenal gland that his guardians ignored, according to police.
articles.body: A Missouri mother and another caretaker have been charged with murder in the death of her emaciated 3-year-old son, who died from cancer in a squalid, roach-infested home two years after doctors found a tumor on his adrenal gland that his guardians ignored, according to police. The child, who was not identified by authorities, had been diagnosed with a neuroblastoma at Children’s Mercy Hospital in Kansas City but was never taken back for the follow-ups that doctors recommended, according to an account in court papers from the Ozark Police Department. Neuroblastoma is a rare cancer of a child’s nerve cells that has a promising survival rate if treated. The malnourished boy’s body was covered with bumps that police initially thought were bruises when they arrived at the Ozark, Missouri, home on July 31, where they found the chilling scene. An autopsy revealed that tumors had developed throughout the toddler’s body, including on his forehead and torso, police said. An obituary announcing the boy’s death painted his family life as rosy and fulfilling. It said he cherished spending time with his siblings, was fond of “PAW Patrol” and enjoyed coloring and crafts. “His favorite thing to do was go to the races on the weekends with his family,” said the funeral home’s announcement, which also dubbed him the “lil troublemaker of the family.” First responders said the boy was emaciated, that he was wearing a dirty diaper, and that he had roaches crawling on his bony right hand when they arrived after his mother reported he was unresponsive, according to court papers. Throughout the house, responders saw “rotting food, insect infestation, animal feces and urine, extreme clutter and trash around the home.” The boy was found “obviously deceased and beyond the help of life-saving measures” when responders first arrived at the home, according to a probable cause statement filed in Christian County court last week. A felony complaint filed against the child’s mother, Destiny Schliefert, on Thursday charges her with second-degree murder, abuse or neglect of a child, endangering the welfare of a child and animal neglect. She is not eligible for bond. Debbie Sue Potter, another woman living in the house who allegedly looked after the victim and other children, is also being held without bail on the same set of charges. The obituary and court records referred to Potter as the boy’s “grammy.” It was not immediately clear whether either woman was represented by a lawyer. A Children’s Mercy Hospital spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Schliefert allegedly offered detectives a litany of excuses for why she didn’t take the boy to the hospital in the days leading up to his death, when she said child Medicaid insurance kicked in following a lapse in coverage, court papers say. Children’s Mercy Hospital offers financial assistance for families who are uninsured or can’t afford treatment. It was “anxiety” that kept her from getting help for the boy shortly before his death, Schliefert told police, the probable cause statement says. Another adult in the home had a fear of blood, and a hospital trip would cause childcare problems for the rest of the kids in the home, Schliefert told investigators. Schliefert also insisted that doctors told her the tumor was benign, which police said was disputed by the children’s hospital physicians who diagnosed him in May 2024, according to the probable cause statement. The hospital told detectives that there were multiple attempts to reach the family after they failed to show up for visits. The statement also says that a detective investigating the abuse and the child’s death asked Schliefert whether she considered calling an ambulance as she watched her son waste away. “I called an ambulance the day he passed away,” Schliefert said, according to court records.

articles.title: Famous bald eagle Lincoln goes rogue before Eagles game, takes an unexpected joy flight
articles.summary: Lincoln, the Budweiser Super Bowl commercial bald eagle, went rogue before the Philadelphia Eagles hosted Pittsburgh Steelers at Lincoln Financial Field.
articles.body: Sometimes, even celebrity bald eagles get the zoomies. Lincoln, the famous bird who stole hearts in Budweiser's Super Bowl commercial earlier this year, apparently decided to go off-script before the Philadelphia Eagles hosted the Pittsburgh Steelers on Sunday. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS The 28-year-old bald eagle, who regularly performs ceremonial flyovers at Lincoln Financial Field, seemingly went rogue during his pregame appearance, taking an unexpected detour instead of sticking to his usual flight routine. Apparently, Lincoln had some extra energy to burn. And while a bald eagle flying wherever he pleases might sound perfectly normal, Lincoln isn't just any bird. He's a highly trained performer who has spent years learning to navigate packed football stadiums, television sets and other environments most wild eagles will never encounter. OutKick OutDoors met Lincoln earlier this year Back in April, OutKick OutDoors visited the American Eagle Foundation in Kodak, Tenn., where Lincoln lives when he's not entertaining NFL crowds or starring in commercials. And having met him myself, I can tell you this bird has personality. There's a certain confidence about him. A lot of attitude. Kind of like he knows America is in love with him. Lincoln was hatched at the American Eagle Foundation in 1998 and initially released into the wild. But despite flying more than 500 miles in his first two weeks, he struggled to hunt and eventually began seeking out humans to give him food. Wildlife officials ultimately determined he couldn't survive on his own, so he returned to the foundation, where he became an ambassador for bald eagle conservation. And, eventually, a pretty big celebrity. His NFL career began in 2024 after years of specialized training, which allows him to fly freely around a stadium packed with more than 65,000 screaming football fans. During our visit, American Eagle Foundation avian care specialist Ryn Cobb explained how that process works. "It's a little complicated, but we basically teach them that food is a rewarding behavior for them," Cobb told OutKick OutDoors. "They understand that when they come to the glove, they get food. And slowly over time, we increase that distance." FIELD NOTES: KOE WETZEL BAGS A TEXAS GIANT, JACOB WHEELER GOES OFFSHORE & A WHALE VISITS NYC So Lincoln isn't tethered during his stadium performances. He's genuinely flying free, and the decision to return to his handler is ultimately his. "We use a GPS system called telemetry that attaches to his ankle and that keeps him safe so we know where he is," Cobb explained. "And he chooses to come home every single time."
